#57. Latest Update: How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter

📅 12 Nov 2026

Latest Update: How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter

Tanggal: 12 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.healthline.com/health-news/kelly-rowland-eczema-flare-ups

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

According to recent reports, wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight. But for those with eczema, this time of year can wreak havoc on their skin, too.

In a recent development, that’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s. During the winter months, she often dreads the cold.

“[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.

Cold weather and indoor heating can reduce humidity, drying out the skin and triggering or worsening eczema flare-ups.

“[What we know] about the skin barrier is that it really is like a gate or wall against the outside world,” Camille Howard-Verovic, MD, a dermatologist at Active Dermatology, told Healthline.

In healthy skin, the barrier controls what enters and leaves the skin. However, for people with eczema, Howard-Verovic said they have skin barrier dysfunction, which allows substances such as allergens and irritants to penetrate the skin.

Cold weather can increase transepidermal water loss, a process in which moisture escapes through the skin’s outer barrier and evaporates into the surrounding air.

Industry observers note that “People with eczema have a tremendous amount of transepidermal water loss, so you’re just drier,” remarked Howard-Verovic. “[You’re] not holding onto the water as well, so that causes the itching and the rash that we feel when we have eczema.”.

Rowland first noticed eczema flares behind her ears as well as on her elbows, arms, and the back of her knees.

“[It] looked like a rash, so that’s what I thought it was all this time, and I dealt with it for so long until after I had my son and then it started to get worse on my face,” she noted.

She eventually went to a dermatologist who diagnosed her with moderate-to-severe eczema, a chronic inflammatory skin condition that can cause intense itching, painful skin cracking, thickened skin, and redness or swelling.

When Rowland learned that eczema can be genetic, it made sense to her.

“I remember seeing significant rashes on [my mom’s] neck and her arms…so she had it, and I guess I was the lucky one,” noted Rowland.

In a recent development, at first, she tried eliminating foods that she thought might be triggers. She also bathed in oatmeal.

“[I] literally have had a tub full of oatmeal, like literally went to the store to get store-bought fresh oats,” she stated. “I tried everything, and it doesn’t help until you go talk to a doctor about it.”.

At first, she tried prescription topical medications but found them cumbersome.

“I don’t have the time, if I’m being honest, and we live in a world that is moving so fast…I started buying like three tubes of whatever it was I was using and losing it; it was just too much for me,” Rowland said.

Industry observers note that rowland said she found relief with Ebglyss, a prescription injectable medication for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. She has also partnered with Eli Lilly and Company, its manufacturer, to raise awareness about eczema.

Rowland said she’s sharing her experience to help others living with eczema, including people she’s met who have experienced greater challenges managing the condition.

“One lady was telling me about how she’s having a tough time [looking] in the mirror cause she doesn’t know who’s looking back at her, and she saw her skin before eczema and after,” noted Rowland.

When she first had symptoms, she noted she felt embarrassed, too.

“[Because] it was just in the middle of my arm space and…[if I] put out my hand to shake someone’s hand, you don’t know if somebody’s judgy,” she mentioned.

Rowland hopes being open about her condition will encourage others to advocate for themselves and talk with their doctor about treatment options.

Because eczema can look different on deeper skin tones, Howard-Verovic noted that a dermatologist can help make the correct diagnosis.

“Some people may not even know that they have eczema,” she stated. “We know that eczema is a rash; it can appear red on certain skin tones, and it can be grey or white on certain skin tones, so it can look a little different.”.

In addition to medication, Rowland stated managing stress helps reduce her eczema flare-ups.

“Before [when] I went on tour, because I was under so much stress, it flared up like crazy, like you wouldn’t believe,” she noted. “We were in the back trying to figure out how to cover certain things up, and we figured some of it out, and some of it was really tricky, but what helped was when I actually just calmed down…not that it helped overnight, but it did just kind of bring the flare down.”.

She said red light therapy, feeling grounded outside without her shoes on, getting vitamin D from natural sunlight, and cooking are ways she reduces ongoing stress.

“Cooking calms me when my kids aren’t here, and I have a really good [Zen] playlist on,” noted Rowland. “[If] you ask me a question [in those moments], I might give you my heart; I’m just so happy.”.

She also tries to cut back on sugar, which she believes triggers flares.

Another way to reduce flares, according to Howard-Verovic, is to avoid hot showers, especially in the winter.

“[We] know eczematous skin likes lukewarm water,” she said.

Because Howard-Verovic and her daughter both live with eczema, she set a rule about when it’s time to get out of the shower.

“[If] you see condensation on the bathroom mirror, you’ve spent too much time in the shower,” said Howard-Verovic. “[That] really hot, hot water feels really good in that moment…but when you get out all that water evaporates, and there’s no moisture in the atmosphere, and it dries your skin out, and now your skin is unhappy again.”.

If you prefer to take baths, she mentioned use gentle cleansers.

“[There] are bleach baths for really, really bad flare-ups,” she noted.

Diluted bleach baths are sometimes recommended for people with eczema, but they should only be used according to a healthcare professional’s instructions.

As soon as you get out of the shower or bath, Howard-Verovic noted to apply a quality moisturizer to your damp skin. According to the National Eczema Association (NEA), lotions containing the following ingredients can help ease dry skin associated with eczema.

To help identify appropriate products, look for ones that have the NEA’s Seal of Acceptance.

#58. America's Top 3 SUVs Are About To Be Hybrid Or Electric

📅 12 Nov 2026

America's Top 3 SUVs Are About To Be Hybrid Or Electric

Tanggal: 12 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://insideevs.com/news/815319/honda-crv-hybrid-toyota-rav4-tesla-model-y/

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Recent moves from Toyota and Honda prove it once and for all: Pure gasoline options just can't hang with electrified power anymore. On Thursday, Honda announced that its best-selling CR-V crossover will be available exclusively as a hybrid starting with a redesigned 2028 model.

"With a 100% hybrid powertrain, the next-generation Honda CR-V will further expand the appeal of America's most popular SUV as demand for hybrid-electric vehicles reaches record levels," said Luis Guerra, assistant vice president of Honda National Auto Sales.

Industry observers note that arriving next year, the 2028 CR-V will kick off a seventh generation for the SUV and be powered exclusively by a new two-motor hybrid system. Honda indicates the tech will boost driving efficiency and expand the range where the engine operates most efficiently, as compared with its current hybrid system. Today, the CR-V is available with both hybrid and pure-combustion powertrains.

Toyota made the RAV4 exclusively a hybrid starting with the 2026 model. Now Honda is following suit.

The Honda news follows similar decisions by Toyota, which made the RAV4 SUV hybrid-only starting with the 2026 model. (The Camry, too, is now only a hybrid.).

Taken together, it means that soon the top three models in the heart of the U.S. car market will come with some form of electrification. That alone will do a lot for getting people into more efficient cars—even if they aren't ready for an EV yet. In 2025, the RAV4, CR-V, and Tesla Model Y were America's best-selling SUVs, responsible for some 1.2 million sales combined.

The move should give a further boost to hybrid sales in America, which have already been on a tear. In the third quarter, hybrids reached 16% of the U.S. light-duty vehicle market. Chalk it up to growing awareness, higher gas prices, and more options in the marketplace.

Those options are poised to grow even further as more automakers capitalize on growing interest in hybrids—particularly in the SUV segment. Nissan is readying a Rogue Hybrid with a unique hybrid system that makes it drive a lot like an EV. GM is reportedly bringing hybrid powertrains to its three-row SUVs, like the Chevy Traverse and GMC Acadia.

In a sense, it's a wonder the hybrid boom didn't happen sooner. Getting a hybrid instead of a gas vehicle is essentially a no-brainer. You may pay a little more up front, but research reveals that the fuel savings over time pay off the difference fairly quickly. According to Consumer Reports, the average hybrid commands a $1,700 premium, but most models pay for themselves within four years.

Industry observers note that just remember: Full EVs are still the cheapest vehicles to run per mile, if you have home charging. They'll always be better for the environment than hybrids too. And the smooth, quiet driving experience is tough to beat. More hybrid Hondas are a step in the right direction, but with the automaker bowing out of the EV game for now, buyers looking to ditch gas entirely will have to look elsewhere.

The Unexpected Legacy of Childhood Adversity

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Recently I attended the 35th anniversary celebrations of Smile as a Gift—Úsmev ako dar—a charitable organization in Bratislava, Slovakia, that assists children in foster care and children’s homes, as well as families threatened by poverty, violence, imprisonment, or illness.

Sources indicate that slovakia also has a Commissioner for Children, Jozef Miklosko, who is committed to defending children’s rights under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Jozef and I spent many hours talking about Slovak “social orphans," children who have been separated from their parents because of a complicated mixture of neglect, poverty, illness, imprisonment, abuse, family breakdown, and, more recently, displacement by the war in Ukraine. They are now under the care of the social welfare system. Each child has a different history and reacts differently to harsh conditions. But they are all affected. What is happening in Slovakia is happening everywhere. Hundreds of millions of children in every country are vulnerable to adversity. Growing up under such stressful conditions undermines health, development, and learning.

Sources indicate that it was only 28 years ago that researchers introduced the concept of adverse childhood experiences, ACEs, as a way of measuring the cumulative effects of childhood adversity. Since then, many studies have shown that ACEs appear to extend across the lifespan, increasing the likelihood of unhealthy behaviors, mental illness, and a range of chronic physical diseases.

In a recent development, professor Karen Hughes of Bangor University in the UK and her colleagues conducted a particularly thorough review. The 37 studies involved more than a quarter of a million people. They found that more childhood hardship increases the risk of widespread challenges later in life. The links were relatively weak for obesity, physical inactivity, and diabetes; stronger for smoking, heavy drinking, cancer, heart disease, and respiratory illness; and stronger still for mental health problems and risky sexual behavior. But the most disturbing associations were with drug misuse, violence toward others, and violence directed against oneself.

Most Abused Children Abuse Others in Adulthood.

Recent findings suggest that surprisingly, the commonly held belief that children who suffer physical abuse are at increased risk of becoming abusive parents themselves, and that children who have been sexually abused become adult sexual offenders is refuted by many academic studies. Most abused children do not grow up to abuse others.

Scientific research focused for a long time on the risks associated with adversity. The prevailing deficit model described children from high-stress backgrounds as being at risk for impairments in learning and behavior. The intervention goal was to prevent, reduce, or repair the damage.

Recent findings suggest that recent studies show that damage and adaptation can occur simultaneously. How do some individuals manage to flourish despite painful experiences that leave others struggling? The following brief biographies may throw some light on the subject that academic studies fail to do.

We are all familiar with Charles Dickens, but most of us don’t know that his father was imprisoned for debt, and at 12, Dickens was sent to work in a shoe-blacking factory. The humiliation and insecurity of that experience haunted him and informed much of his writing. He made the suffering of impoverished children one of the great moral themes of his writing.

Abraham Lincoln’s childhood was marked by poverty, exhausting physical labour, and limited schooling. When Lincoln was 9, his mother died. His father remarried a widow with three children. Lucky for young Abe, his stepmother was not the folkloric evil stepmother but a significant positive influence. She encouraged his love of books, treated him affectionately; they shared a close relationship for the rest of her life.

Sources indicate that although their childhoods differed considerably, Charles Dickens, Abraham Lincoln, and many others I don’t have space to mention spent their childhoods in environments that offered limited educational opportunities. However, they shared an awareness of the limitations of their present lives and found people who encouraged them and helped them to progress. Their childhood experiences shaped what they noticed, cared about, and fought for.

Sources indicate that in some instances, having been powerless may make a person particularly aware of the powerlessness of others. Unfair treatment may motivate some individuals to commit to fair play and justice.

While we cannot deny that adversity, especially early adversity, has a corrosive effect, it is equally true that some people, like the ones mentioned here and thousands of others, have overcome and grown from it.

Childhood Adversity Requires More Than Individual Resilience.

ACE research shows how experience becomes embedded in our biology and psyche—how childhood becomes embodied.

Sources indicate that recovery from adversity is not about forgetting or papering over the hurts and wounds. Such recovery often takes place in a residential setting, a safe place where truly dedicated and caring people provide many opportunities for reparenting, developing trust, good communication, education, counselling, and a variety of workshops such as those on forgiveness that can help patients grow into the healthy adults they were meant to be. Individual resilience is not enough. Children need people and institutions that give them opportunities to recover.

Sources indicate that adversity is not a witch’s curse, as in Sleeping Beauty; it is not destiny. It is also not necessarily ennobling. It is not one or the other. The human mind is complex. Someone may be highly successful professionally and a failure at personal relationships. Another may struggle with anxiety or depression yet be remarkably generous and compassionate.

It has been revealed that you may ask: Do I carry any scars from my childhood? And if so, how have they affected me?

Recent findings suggest that in many cases, adversity predates birth. I shall address that in my next post.

#62. High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Reveals

High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Reveals

Tanggal: 12 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.healthline.com/health-news/high-fat-diet-may-increase-colon-cancer-risk-study

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a upcoming study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.

The researchers from Arizona State University noted a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.

The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.

The researchers published their findings on November 12 in the journal Stem Cell Reports.

According to recent reports, the researchers said the study is important because 1 in 25 people develop colon cancer in their lifetime. In the United States, that translates into about 108,000 fresh cases of colon cancer every year. About 55,000 males and 55,000 females are expected to die from the disease in 2026.

Experts not involved in the study say the research provides valuable information, but they have reservations about the results, as the findings do not yet apply to humans.

“The findings provide a potential mechanism linking diet to intestinal cancer development, but we need to be cautious about translating these results to humans,” mentioned Dalia Perelman, MS, CDE, a research dietitian at Stanford University in California.

Industry observers note that “We already have evidence from human studies that obesity and certain dietary patterns, particularly those high in processed meats and low in fiber-rich foods, are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk,” Perelman told Healthline. “This study adds a potentially vital mechanism to investigate, but it does not establish that dietary fat itself increases colorectal cancer risk in humans.”.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, shared similar views.

“This study provides a better understanding at the cellular level of how a high fat diet may contribute to colorectal cancer development,” Thanki told Healthline.

“Animal studies are an important starting point for understanding biological processes, but we must be cautious about directly applying their findings to humans,” he added. “Mice and humans share many cellular and biological mechanisms, which makes these studies valuable in identifying potential pathways involved in disease development. However, human diets, genetics, metabolism, and environmental exposures are more complex.”.

To reach their findings, the Arizona State researchers fed mice what the scientists described as a Western-style high fat diet for 6 months.

They then compared those results with those from mice given a low fat diet.

Industry observers note that the researchers mentioned the mice on the high fat diet gained more weight than the mice on the low-fat diet. They also developed more intestinal stem cells, and those cells grew at a more rapid rate.

They added that mice genetically predisposed to intestinal cancer who were fed a high-fat diet developed more and larger tumors.

The researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may help explain their increased growth and survival.

They also pointed out that stem cell behavior returned to normal after high fat diet mice were switched to a low fat diet, although some DNA changes persisted. After four weeks, approximately 18% of these changes remained.

When mice were returned to a high fat diet, the researchers noted their intestinal stem cells responded more rapidly and strongly than those of mice exposed to the diet for the first time.

They concluded that the study suggests that maintaining a healthy, low fat diet may help regulate intestinal stem cell growth and reduce colon cancer risk.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, RD, president of KAK Consulting and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Ohio, wasn’t involved in the study but highlighted a particular aspect of the findings.

“What I found particularly interesting was that even after the mice returned to a low fat diet, some of the molecular changes persisted,” she told Healthline. “This raises questions about how our dietary patterns over time may influence long-term health.”.

Experts said these upcoming findings are interesting but noted numerous caveats.

Sources indicate that “One notable takeaway is that dietary habits over time matter,” remarked Thanki. “Even if someone has consumed a high fat diet for years, making changes now may still provide meaningful health benefits.”.

“I also think these findings are particularly important for children and adolescents, as establishing healthier dietary habits early in life may provide long-term benefits,” he added.

However, Thanki noted that not all fats are the same. “The health risks depend partly on the type of fat consumed, how much is consumed, and what foods make up the overall diet,” he said.

“Diets consistently high in saturated fats, particularly those containing large amounts of processed meats, fried foods, and highly processed products, can contribute to obesity, elevated cholesterol, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction. These factors can also contribute to chronic inflammation and may increase the risk of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer,” Thanki continued.

Perelman mentioned the diet used in the study was extremely high in fat, providing 60% of calories from fat, primarily from lard.

“We know that the health effects of dietary fats differ depending on their sources and fatty acid composition, and we cannot assume that a diet rich in unsaturated fats from foods such as olive oil, nuts, and seeds would produce the same effects,” she noted.

Perelman added that the researchers primarily studied stem cells from the small intestine rather than the colon.

“Although these tissues share some biological characteristics, they have important differences, and we cannot assume that the same changes would occur in the colon,” she explained.

Finally, Perelman noted that “the mice consuming the high fat diet also gained weight, making it difficult to separate the effects of dietary fat itself from those associated with increased body fat and other metabolic changes.”.

Industry observers note that not all high fat foods are unhealthy. Some high fat foods that offer healthy benefits include:.

“The goal shouldn’t necessarily be to eliminate fat because our bodies need healthy fats for normal functioning,” remarked Thanki. “Instead, people should focus on reducing saturated and trans fats while incorporating healthier unsaturated fats in appropriate amounts.”.

Thanki had several dietary suggestions. Among them:.

In a recent development, “Consistency matters more than perfection. Even modest dietary changes, maintained over time, can have meaningful health benefits,” Thanki stated.

In a recent development, perelman agreed. “The overall quality of the diet matters. Diets that are very high in fat may displace other foods and nutrients that have key health benefits,” she remarked.

“For colorectal cancer specifically, higher intakes of dietary fiber and whole grains have consistently been associated with lower risk,” Perelman noted.

“Therefore, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing fat, it is vital to consider the overall dietary pattern and whether it provides adequate amounts of fiber-rich plant foods and other beneficial nutrients.”.

In a recent development, kirkpatrick agreed that the type of fat is what is crucial. “A Mediterranean-style diet that includes olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish can be relatively high in fat but is consistently associated with positive health outcomes,” she said.

“On the other hand, a diet high in saturated fat, processed meats, and ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of certain chronic diseases, particularly when it’s also low in fiber and other protective nutrients.”.

Kirkpatrick also noted that many lifestyle habits contribute to a person’s overall health.

“Our health is influenced by so many factors beyond diet, including how we manage stress, our sleep habits, physical activity, genetics, and overall lifestyle,” she said.

#65. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

📅 13 Nov 2026

Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261111005911.htm

In a recent development, A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an notable difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

According to recent reports, the medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns.

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

Industry observers note that "GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens.".

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies.

It has been revealed that the research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk.

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, stated the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely crucial findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association.".

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs.

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure crucial differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant.".

Although the results provide useful fresh information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In a recent development, in particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish fresh clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Crucial Limitations of the Pregnancy Study.

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

According to recent reports, however, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs.".

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance.

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

Industry observers note that in an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs.".

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

Sources indicate that "For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy.".

Industry observers note that ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

#66. 1 in 3 Infants Diagnosed With Peanut Allergy May Not Have the Condition

📅 11 Nov 2026

1 in 3 Infants Diagnosed With Peanut Allergy May Not Have the Condition

Tanggal: 11 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.healthline.com/health-news/many-infants-diagnosed-with-peanut-allergy-may-not-have-condition

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.

According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.

However, new research published in the November 2026 matter of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.

In fact, having a history of reacting to peanuts and positive allergy testing on their own may not be sufficient to diagnose a peanut allergy for many infants.

The study’s authors suggest that a threshold oral food challenge — in which the child is given increasing amounts of the suspected food allergen under medical supervision to look for an allergic reaction — should be routinely considered to help confirm peanut allergy.

This additional testing could safely prevent children who are not allergic to peanuts from undergoing unnecessary treatment with oral immunotherapy.

It could also spare families from burdensome food restrictions and allergy precautions.

The researchers’ goal was to evaluate the accuracy and safety of the Allergy Development to an Accelerated Path to Tolerance (ADAPT) peanut oral immunotherapy program, which was established in 2024 at 10 public children’s hospitals across Australia.

This program provides a standardized approach to evaluating and treating infants with suspected peanut allergies.

The study included infants who had experienced a mild to moderate reaction to peanut before 12 months of age and had evidence of peanut sensitization through allergy testing.

Researchers reviewed medical records to examine how accurately the program’s approach identified peanut allergies and whether it could safely guide treatment.

A key part of the evaluation was a threshold oral food challenge. The challenge involved up to seven doses, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams of peanut protein.

Medical teams monitored the infants for reactions and provided treatment when necessary.

In a recent development, researchers reviewed records from April 2024 through October 2025. During that period, 1,275 infants were assessed through the program, and 778 underwent an oral food challenge.

The researchers also examined allergy test results and whether infants who reacted during the challenges could begin oral immunotherapy at an appropriate starting dose.

At the time of the oral food challenge, the infants had a median age of 13 months.

Of the 778 infants who underwent an oral food challenge, 507 (65.2%) had an allergic reaction.

However, 271 (34.8%) did not react to peanut during the supervised test, despite having a history of a previous reaction and positive allergy test results.

These findings suggest that relying on medical history and allergy tests alone may lead some infants to be labeled with a peanut allergy when they can actually tolerate the food.

Among the infants who reacted during the challenges, 61 experienced anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. This represented 12% of infants with a positive challenge and 7.8% of all infants who underwent testing. Medical teams safely managed these severe allergic reactions.

Researchers also found that infants who reacted to peanut generally had higher skin prick test results and Ara h 2-specific IgE levels than those who did not react.

However, these test results did not reliably indicate how much peanut would trigger a reaction or how severe that reaction would be.

Of the 394 infants who began peanut oral immunotherapy, 384 (97.5%) successfully started treatment at a dose below the amount that had triggered a reaction during their food challenge.

The researchers say these findings support considering supervised oral food challenges to confirm suspected peanut allergies before starting treatment or recommending long-term avoidance.

Erin Banta, MD, a board certified allergist and immunologist who treats both children and adults at Latitude Food Allergy Care in Great Neck, New York, remarked these findings are significant because they provide evidence for early use of oral food challenges in infants with peanut reactions.

“In those with mild-moderate prior reactions to peanut, early oral food challenge may allow for either delabeling of food allergy (in 1/3 of the patients in this study) or diagnosis of food allergy,” she told Healthline.

Banta, who wasn’t involved in the study, added that early delabeling takes a significant burden off the patient and their family.

“On the other hand,” she explained, “early diagnosis allows for early initiation of treatment with oral immunotherapy at a time in the patient’s life associated with the greatest success rates.”.

Banta further noted that the study offers different pathways for oral immunotherapy based on the patient’s reaction threshold. This means that some patients may be able to complete treatment more promptly due to their individual threshold dose.

Lindsey Forstie, FNP, a family nurse practitioner with clinical training and experience in allergy and asthma care at Carefree Allergy in Phoenix, AZ, added that while further evaluation may be needed to confirm a peanut allergy diagnosis, it’s key for parents not to try introducing peanuts at home.

“Instead, they should speak with their pediatrician or allergist about appropriate testing and whether a supervised food challenge is safe and necessary,” she stated.

According to Forstie, who was also not part of the study, the goal is to avoid unnecessary food restrictions while also keeping children safe.

Sources indicate that “The key message is that not every positive allergy test means a child has a food allergy,” she told Healthline. “Accurate diagnosis helps protect children while allowing those who are not allergic to enjoy a more normal, less restrictive diet.”.

Industry observers note that BYD has already shown that charging an EV doesn’t have to take much longer than filling a gas tank. Now it’s tackling another problem: getting enough electricity to a fast charger in the first place.

Its upcoming site in the Abu Dhabi desert combines solar panels, battery storage, Flash Charging, and a robotic arm that plugs in the car. BYD notes the system can work independently of the electricity grid, potentially bringing fast charging to places where a power connection may not be feasible. The proposition is pretty simple: Solar panels generate electricity, batteries store it, and the charger sends it to an EV.

Battery-backed charging is becoming more common because it lets stations deliver more power than their grid connection alone can supply, while also reducing demand on the grid during busy periods. Tesla’s biggest Supercharger site, which it opened earlier this year, also uses solar panels and Tesla's Megapack batteries. Companies like Electric Era and Beam Global specialize in battery-backed charging. Even BYD Flash chargers not located in the middle of the desert and not supplied by solar panels use on-site energy storage to boost power delivery.

Each of BYD's T-shaped Flash chargers is hooked up to two 185-kilowatt-hour storage batteries, for 370 kWh total. These draw power from the grid at around 100 to 560 kilowatts, then supply the car at a much higher rate. The chargers can send up to 1,500 kW through one cable, or up to 1,000 kW when both are in use at the same time.

Adding solar panels into the equation means some or even all of that electricity can be generated on-site. However, BYD hasn’t disclosed the battery capacity or solar output of this latest desert installation. So it's not clear how many cars the station can charge—or how quickly—on solar power alone.

The charging hardware is impressively quick. With BYD’s latest 1,500-kW Flash chargers, compatible cars running its second-generation Blade battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or hit 97% in nine minutes.

Now that infrastructure is going global. The company notes it plans to establish 6,000 Flash Charging stations worldwide by the end of 2027, but it hasn’t specified how many will offer solar power, off-grid operation, or that robotic arm.

Europe is getting a taste of BYD’s Flash charging with sites up and running in Italy, Germany, France, and the United Kingdom. Canada is coming soon too. The only vehicle it currently sells in Europe that can fully utilize its power is the Denza Z9 GT. During a demonstration, the electric wagon charged from 10% to 80% in six minutes and 32 seconds, reaching 97% in nine minutes and 22 seconds.

How the 'Dune' director turned a little-known short story into one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century.

In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In "Star Trek", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication.

In a recent development, but in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.

The film's journey to the big screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest.

"It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline. "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'".

So when 21 Laps (the production firm that later went on to make "Stranger Things") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten.

"I was so excited, but I had that dread that a lot of producers get, which is, 'Are the rights available?'" 21 Laps' Dan Levine told the Hollywood Gold podcast. "You read something that blows you away, and then you find there aren't the rights, and there's no chance, you have to move on. So we were trying to track down this Ted Chiang, and he had no agent. He had a day job. He was impossible to find, so we started the hunt for Ted Chiang.".

In a recent development, an up-and-coming Canadian director named Denis Villeneuve had also found his way on to 21 Laps' radar after his 2010 French-language drama "Incendies" earned rave reviews and an Academy Award nomination. He told the producers that he'd always wanted to direct a science fiction film — a hint of things to come? — and they indicated him "Story of Your Life".

In a recent development, he was also drawn to the story, while the now-located Chiang was suitably impressed by the director's work on "Incendies" to make a deal for the rights. And with Amy Adams also interested in playing the lead role of linguist Dr Louise Banks, the film that would eventually become "Arrival" was ready to proceed — or, at least, it would be once Villeneuve had completed his first three Hollywood movies, "Prisoners" (2013), "Enemy" (2013) and "Sicario" (2015).

With 12 alien spaceships arriving simultaneously around the globe, "Arrival"'s poster-friendly elevator pitch could almost have been borrowed from "Independence Day". Indeed, the question of whether these whisper-quiet, chocolate button-shaped craft belong to the "Day the Earth Stood Still" / "Close Encounters" friendly extraterrestrial camp, or have the invasion of planet Earth on their minds is a mystery the world's governments are desperate to solve.

"Denis didn't really see this as an alien invasion movie — more an alien arrival movie," producer Aaron Ryder told SFX magazine. "What would be the protocols that were in place? How would they be implemented? How would people react? What would the government be doing? What would the news organisations be saying? That was the tone and the texture, which is established right up front.".

These Hollywood blockbuster components were not part of "Story of Your Life". But even though Heisserer's script was not a direct translation of Chiang's tale, he retained the most crucial bits — namely Dr Banks' efforts to establish a means of communication with seven-legged extraterrestrial heptapods, and the profound effect their language has on her perception of time.

Designed by Carlos Huante, the heptapods themselves are like giant elongated hands, alien visitors light years away from the "Star Trek" tradition of actors with a few ridges glued to their foreheads. Like the evil 456 in "Torchwood: Children of Earth", they're enclosed in gaseous chambers and make sounds imperceptible to the human ear.

This, however, is where "Arrival" gets really interesting. Working alongside physicist colleague Dr Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner), Banks gradually exchanges foundational vocabulary with two heptapods they name Abbott and Costello. They discover that the alien visitors use a sophisticated written language of circular "logograms", squirted into their atmosphere as if it were sentient squid ink.

Recent findings suggest that "The idea in the short story is of circular language that has no beginning and no end," Villeneuve explained in an interview with IndieWire. "We were looking for no relation to any human language. I had to figure out how to produce logograms from my aliens while avoiding being long and boring. The sounds were an expression of their emotions, with more intellect coming from the signs. This beautiful species uses written language as their first means of expression instead of movement or gesture. They produce words out of their bodies.".

In a recent development, but Banks and Donnelly's research project has a purpose. With the world's military on high alert — and, ironically, struggling to communicate — they need to work out how to ask the aliens a fundamental question: Why are you here?

According to recent reports, the heptapods' answer — "offer weapon" — is tantalizingly ambiguous. Are they planning to attack? Or is, as Banks suggests, 'weapon' simply being used as a synonym for 'tool'?

In a recent development, aside from a bomb planted on the heptapod ship by a rogue US soldier, "Arrival" is mostly free from the big-budget explosions that are part-and-parcel of most alien visitation movies. Instead, the film's denouement delivers a twist — the crux of Chiang's story — that rivals "The Sixth Sense", "Fight Club" and "The Prestige" in its audacious sleight of hand.

It turns out the "weapon" in question is actually the heptapod language, which, thanks to their non-linear perception of time, gives speakers a unique perspective on the past, present, and future. Therefore, those scenes we assumed to be flashbacks to the life and tragic death of Louise's daughter, Hannah, are actually flashforwards, as her increased understanding of heptapod-speak gives her memories of a life she hasn't yet lived.

Villeneuve put on multiple test screenings to ensure the big reveals hit properly.

"I wanted to screen it with people who knew nothing about the project," he noted. "What we discovered is when someone in the audience felt too lost — if intellectually they were not engaged — the ending was less powerful from an emotional point of view. So we tried to give as few clues as possible, but enough clues to be able to stay engaged and follow the story.".

According to recent reports, those subtle hints become obvious on second and third viewings, whether it's a lingering shot of a wedding ring absent in the movie's "present" or a conversation about the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (the notion that the structure of a language can influence the way its speakers think). The absence of young Hannah's father also takes on tragic upcoming meaning when we realize it's Ian, who'll leave after Louise tells him about their daughter's sad fate.

"We were walking on this tightrope of trying to play things so it could play both ways, because of the reveal at the end," Adams recalled in a Vanity Fair conversation with Villeneuve. "I had to do so much work to understand how I play a character so that the first time you watch it you think that it's one thing, and the second time you watch it you can see it from a totally different perspective.".

Sources indicate that while Adams didn't get the Oscar nomination her performance deserved, everything else paid off, with the film making over $200 million worldwide from its reported $47 million budget. (The film did win an Academy Award for sound editing, while receiving further nods for best picture, director, and adapted screenplay.).

Villeneuve has famously gone on to become Hollywood's go-to guy for intelligent sci-fi, thanks to "Blade Runner 2049" and the smash-hit "Dune" saga, and will next be given the opportunity to resurrect James Bond.

Normally we'd take this opportunity to say no one could have foreseen Villeneuve's subsequent ascendancy but — in a story involving heptapods and some clever people at 21 Laps — who can be so sure?

#69. The Good News About the Midterm Election

📅 13 Nov 2026

The Good News About the Midterm Election

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/thinking-socially/202611/the-good-news-about-the-midterm-election

Industry observers note that after years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Sources indicate that self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Industry observers note that democrats are understandably celebrating the “blue wave” that overtook the U.S. in the midterm election, and many Republicans are stunned and disappointed by the magnitude of their losses. Neither response is surprising, of course. However, as a political psychologist, I can’t help but feel that the results should give hope to all Americans, regardless of political leaning. Let me explain why.

For the past couple of decades, pundits have lamented the polarization of American politics. The conventional wisdom has been that we now live in two Americas, one red and one blue, and that never the twain shall meet. Stereotypes of affluent, educated, urban, wine-drinking liberals and working-class, rural, less-educated, beer-drinking, gun-toting conservatives proliferated. Politics seemed to have become a major dividing line between us.

In a recent development, some political scientists maintained that most Americans are pragmatic moderates and that the level of polarization had been exaggerated, but most media coverage seemed to ignore that point of view. A more nuanced approach suggested that although glitch polarization (differences in policy positions) was less pronounced, affective polarization (feelings toward those in the other party) was indeed extreme. In fact, one study documented that hostility toward those in the other political wing was so great that individuals would be more upset about their offspring marrying someone of the other party than marrying someone of a different race. Given the magnitude of the racial divide in the U.S., that was a remarkable finding.

In a recent development, this take on America as a deeply polarized society has some scary implications for our democracy. Democratic nations function successfully when the voters can be counted on to evaluate politicians and their policies. If polarization is so high that voters always approve of the politicians in their own party and disapprove of the ones in the other party, regardless of their actions, then we have a situation in which our government has no accountability. This would mean that politicians would have guaranteed support from their base no matter what. Why even have elections if they end up simply reflecting a count of the number of people in each party? A government of the people and for the people requires that the people pay attention and fairly evaluate whether our leaders are leading us in the right direction.

The recent election indicated that many people who had been supportive of President Trump and his party changed their minds. Their concerns about complications like affordability, an unpopular war in Iran, an extreme crackdown on immigrants suspected of being undocumented, financial support for what some consider a genocide in Gaza, to name a few, ended up outweighing their desire to stick with the party they had put in power. Painful as this might seem to Republicans, I would argue that it is better for the country as a whole to have an electorate that does not reflexively vote the same way in every election if there are significant reasons to endorse a change. We have to be able to count on the voters to hold our government accountable.

In American culture, to hold someone accountable is to view them as responsible or to blame for a problem. Extensive research has shown that blame plays a major role in politics. Politicians who are blamed, particularly for the state of the economy and war, tend to pay a price in elections. One of the keys to Trump’s success has been an ability to avoid blame for his actions. Recall his statement during a 2016 campaign rally that he could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot someone and wouldn’t lose any voters. Whether one supports Trump or not, it would be hard to argue that allowing a politician to get away with anything is a good practice. Again, accountability is key to democracy.

Sources indicate that therefore, it would seem to be a positive sign that voters, many of whom hold the president responsible for the problems our country faces, are holding him to account. It means that they are actually thinking about the administration’s policies and evaluating them. Wouldn’t we rather have an electorate that bases its voting on such evaluations instead of reflexively voting for the same person they voted for last time, regardless of the state of the country?

Sources indicate that given the general assumption that the U.S. is involved in a war between red and blue value systems, it is perhaps not surprising that a number of Republican candidates focused on hot-button culture war issues like gender roles, LGBTQ+ rights, and DEI efforts in their campaigns. The goal was to convince Americans that some Democrats do not share mainstream American values. For example, James Talarico was attacked as a “woke” vegan who believes in multiple genders. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed was labeled a jihadist who supported the 9/11 attacks. Such rhetoric is aimed at labeling some candidates as “them” rather than “us” and thereby alienating American voters. Interestingly, that approach does not seem to have succeeded, and it may even have backfired. Though there are a number of possible explanations for this trend, a major factor was likely that American voters are much more focused on the economy and therefore do not pay much attention to such attacks. A more optimistic view is that stereotypes and prejudice do not carry the same power they once did. It is also possible that citizens are simply tired of these types of personal attacks. All three of these possibilities speak well of American voters.

According to recent reports, in spite of increased political polarization in the U.S., polls indicate that Americans believe there is more that unites than divides us. It thus stands to reason that we would value an emphasis on unity and civility over division and ugliness. Although the verdict is still out on the degree to which disgust with the nastiness of politics had a role in this election, some pundits have suggested that it was a factor. Most people would likely prefer that politicians focus on the real problems we face as a society rather than tearing each other down.

Recent findings suggest that particularly notable in this regard was Vivek Ramaswamy’s cruel ad attacking the honesty of Dr. Amy Acton. Although some politicians might relish opportunities to verbally attack their opponents in hopes of instilling fear or revulsion in voters, it appears that many Americans are not buying what they are selling. Ramaswamy’s attack resulted in an outpouring of support for Dr. Acton, and she won the election. An attempt to elicit distrust of Dr. Acton actually gave rise to empathy for her.

Shouldn’t we all prefer civility over nastiness and cruelty, regardless of our political leaning? A number of Republicans were among the critics of Ramaswamy’s ad, suggesting that they are capable of holding fellow partisans accountable and that they would prefer more civil politics.

Industry observers note that overall, we can be more optimistic that our democracy, which has become increasingly threatened by intense hostility across party lines, extreme within-party loyalty, a refusal to hold politicians accountable, divisive culture wars, racial and religious prejudice, and a shocking level of incivility, might be moving in a healthy direction. Hopefully, this trend will continue, and our society can live up to its promise.

Every example now features gloss-black 19-inch wheels and mirror caps, and the Brembo-branded brake calipers are now painted yellow. There are no powertrain changes, so a rowdy 320-hp 2.0-liter turbo four and sweet-shifting six-speed manual transmission still feed the front wheels.

Sources indicate that inside, Acura now makes the door-panel trim, door handles, and shift boot dark gray, and that applies to the dashboard too, which also adopts a latest diamond pattern. The three knobs that control the climate settings are now all gloss black, and Acura indicates it has redesigned the upholstery options. The Red and Orchid (white) themes feature faux-suede accents that are black and blue, respectively, but the Ebony option features yellow stitching, which extends to the steering wheel, door panels, and shift boot. The driver’s seat now has memory settings, as does the brake-hold feature, and both exterior mirrors tilt down when the car is put into reverse.

According to recent reports, if you missed your chance to buy a Phoenix Yellow Integra Type R back in the day, Acura is turning back the clock and giving you another shot. Sure, the upcoming Type S model has an extra pair of doors and put on some weight, but it remains one of our favorite driver’s cars, and the Heritage Edition is the only way to get the new Blazing Phoenix Yellow paint job (at least for the ‘27 model year). Not only is the new retro-themed Type S the first Integra with yellow paint since the 2001 Type R, but it also features exclusive copper-colored wheels. Its interior color is limited to the black-and-yellow theme offered on other new Type S models, but the Heritage Edition alone has a titanium shift knob—same as the Honda Civic Type R.

See all results for latest 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 68008.

Acura states the 2027 versions of the Integra Type S will reach dealerships sometime next month. While that includes the newly introduced Heritage Edition, it’s limited to just 700 examples for U.S. audiences. For those who are lucky enough to score one, it’s only $2300 more than the regular Type S, which starts at $55,995.

It has been revealed that eric Stafford’s automobile addiction began before he could walk, and it has fueled his passion to write news, reviews, and more for Car and Driver since 2016. His aspiration growing up was to become a millionaire with a Jay Leno–like car collection. Apparently, getting rich is harder than social-media influencers make it seem, so he avoided financial success entirely to become an automotive journalist and drive new cars for a living. After earning a journalism degree at Central Michigan University and working at a daily newspaper, the years of basically burning money on failed project cars and lemon-flavored jalopies finally paid off when Car and Driver hired him. His garage right now includes a 2010 Acura RDX, a manual '97 Chevy Camaro Z/28, and a '90 Honda CRX Si.
