#116. Tech Report: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

📅 13 Nov 2026

Tech Report: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261111005901.htm

Recent findings suggest that for decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history. That long-standing assumption is now facing newly introduced scrutiny. Observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which is constructing the largest three-dimensional map of the Universe, suggest that dark energy's influence may have changed over billions of years. Although the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish a discovery, it has renewed interest in a fundamental question: Could dark energy evolve rather than remain constant?

Sources indicate that researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity. In a 2025 study published in Physical Review D, an international team led by Prof. Özgür Akarsu of ITU's Department of Physics investigated a mathematical possibility that previous researchers had largely overlooked. Their analysis revealed a surprising scenario in which the effective density of dark energy was negative during the Universe's early history before eventually becoming positive.

The research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr. N. Merve Uzun and doctoral student Bilal Bulduk. The team also collaborated with Prof. Nihan Katırcı of Doğuş University, who previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in Akarsu's group, and Prof. Antonio De Felice of Kyoto University's Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics, an internationally recognized center for theoretical physics.

An Overlooked Possibility in Einstein's Theory of Gravity.

The discovery came from examining a part of an existing theory that had received relatively little attention. Rather than proposing an entirely fresh explanation for dark energy, the researchers revisited a framework known as teleparallel f(T) gravity.

Sources indicate that einstein's general theory of relativity explains gravity through the curvature of spacetime. Teleparallel gravity takes a different mathematical approach, describing gravity through a property called torsion. Scientists have spent years studying modified versions of this framework to investigate whether gravity itself might account for the Universe's accelerating expansion.

Sources indicate that earlier investigations of an exponential form of teleparallel gravity had concentrated on one particular set of mathematical solutions. This approach reflected a familiar assumption inherited from general relativity: dark energy should always have a positive density.

Sources indicate that akarsu and his colleagues decided to investigate what would happen if that restriction were removed. By considering a previously neglected branch of the theory, they uncovered a substantially different picture of how the Universe might have evolved.

Dark Energy May Have Switched From Negative to Positive.

The team's calculations showed that two distinct cosmic histories could emerge even when the Universe contains the same amount of matter today.

According to recent reports, one mathematical solution closely resembles the standard model of cosmology. The other predicts that effective dark energy had a negative density in the distant past. According to this second possibility, the density reached zero at approximately redshift 1.5, corresponding to roughly 9.5 billion years ago, before becoming positive and remaining that way.

What makes the result particularly interesting is that the researchers did not need to introduce an additional adjustable parameter to produce this behavior. Instead, the determining factor is related to the Universe's present matter density, which selects the mathematical branch. As a result, the model retains the same six cosmological parameters used in the standard ΛCDM model.

Sources indicate that the theory also avoids an key potential problem. Although it predicts behavior that differs from Einstein's gravity across enormous cosmic distances, its departures from general relativity become naturally suppressed in dense environments. This allows the alternative solution to remain compatible with the highly accurate measurements of gravity made throughout the Solar System.

A Possible Explanation for the Hubble Tension.

The newly introduced findings build on years of research into whether dark energy could have changed sign during the Universe's history.

Industry observers note that akarsu and his collaborators previously developed a framework called the sign-switching ΛCDM (ΛsCDM) model. In this scenario, the cosmological constant changes from negative to positive several billion years after the Major Bang.

According to recent reports, previous analyses found that a change in the sign of dark energy's density could agree with DESI observations while potentially reducing several unresolved disagreements in cosmology. One of the most significant is the Hubble tension, the persistent discrepancy between different methods of measuring the Universe's present expansion rate.

However, an vital question remained unanswered. What underlying physical process could cause dark energy to undergo such a reversal?

The latest research offers a possible mechanism. Instead of requiring scientists to prescribe a sign change as part of the model, the reversal arises naturally from the mathematical structure of the modified gravity theory.

Akarsu explained why investigating an overlooked solution proved so valuable.

It has been revealed that "For several years we have been studying a scenario in which dark energy switches sign, and it has held up remarkably well against data such as DESI's. The open question was what physical mechanism could produce such behavior. So we deliberately looked at a branch of a well-known theory of gravity that had been set aside because it violates the usual expectation that the dark energy density stays positive. The sign change emerged naturally from the theory itself.".

DESI Observations Raise Fresh Questions About Dark Energy.

The theoretical findings have become especially relevant as astronomers gather increasingly detailed measurements of cosmic expansion.

DESI tracks the locations of millions of galaxies and quasars, allowing researchers to reconstruct how the Universe has expanded across billions of years. In March 2025, the DESI collaboration released findings based on its first three years of observations.

When combined with measurements of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and weak gravitational lensing, the results strengthened earlier indications that dark energy might not behave like a fixed cosmological constant.

These findings do not yet establish that dark energy changes over time. The statistical significance depends on which observational datasets are combined, and the evidence remains below the threshold required to claim a definitive discovery. Nevertheless, the possibility has motivated scientists to investigate alternative descriptions of cosmic expansion.

DESI has now completed its planned five-year survey, observing more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. The complete dataset will provide an even more demanding test of whether the apparent changes in dark energy persist as measurements become more precise.

Sources indicate that the timing is also noteworthy. The ITU-led team's research was initially submitted in October 2024, several months before DESI announced its March 2025 findings. The researchers have not yet tested their model against the complete DESI dataset, making that comparison an notable next step.

Could the Universe's Accelerating Expansion Be Slowing?

The significance of the proposed model extends beyond its prediction that dark energy's density may have changed sign.

In a recent development, because the alternative solution emerges from a specific theory of gravity, it makes predictions about both cosmic expansion and how gravity behaves across the Universe. These predictions give astronomers ways to investigate whether the proposed cosmic history is consistent with observations.

Measurements of how galaxies and larger structures form and grow will be particularly important. Researchers can also examine how gravity bends light and how the Universe's expansion has changed over time. Among the most useful observational tests are structure growth, redshift-space distortions, and weak gravitational lensing.

Although comprehensive testing remains necessary, the initial results offer reasons for further investigation.

In an extended version of the theory that includes a cosmological constant, the researchers found that the model could remain consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background while allowing the higher present-day expansion rates obtained from local measurements. This makes it a potentially useful approach to understanding the Hubble tension.

The extended model also permits another intriguing possibility: the acceleration of the Universe's expansion could have weakened or even stopped in the relatively recent cosmic past. Recent studies examining DESI observations have raised similar questions about whether cosmic acceleration has remained steady.

Industry observers note that importantly, neither the proposed dark energy reversal nor a recent slowdown in cosmic acceleration has been established as an observational fact. Both remain possibilities that must be tested against increasingly precise data.

Revisiting Gravity Could Reveal a Different Cosmic History.

The research highlights how familiar scientific theories can contain possibilities that were missed because earlier investigations relied on restrictive assumptions.

In this case, allowing effective dark energy to have a negative density exposed an alternative evolutionary history within an already established mathematical framework. The researchers suggest that examining similarly overlooked solutions in other modified gravity theories could lead to additional insights.

Ultimately, the strength of the latest explanation will depend on how well it reproduces the Universe astronomers actually observe. The full DESI dataset and other cosmological measurements will help determine whether this unusual version of cosmic history deserves a place alongside established explanations.

"We identified an alternative path for the Universe within an existing theory. The next step is to test it rigorously against the full observational data. The preliminary picture is encouraging, and we are particularly interested in what it may tell us about the Hubble tension," remarked Prof. Özgür Akarsu.

Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star.

According to recent reports, the white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153.

It has been revealed that GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, noted in a statement. "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself.".

The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star.

It has been revealed that "As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, noted. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away.".

Hurley-Walker and the team at ICRAR have been at the cutting edge of rare star systems like this.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia," Hurley-Walker said. "We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position.".

After the radio telescopes detected this LPT, it was confirmed using the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The visible light follow-up of Keck also confirmed that the star in GPM J071507−114153 was a G-type star, just like the sun.

Recent findings suggest that meerKAT and the MWA are both precursors for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world’s largest and most sensitive radio telescope project. That means the future is bright for LPTs.

"If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKA telescopes are completely built," McSweeney mentioned.

The team's research was published on Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

#122. Music as an Intervention in Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy

📅 13 Nov 2026

Music as an Intervention in Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/modern-medicine/202611/music-as-an-intervention-in-psychedelic-assisted-therapy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

It has been revealed that self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Industry observers note that music has long been part of ceremonial and healing practices involving psychedelics, and it has played a role in Western psychedelic research for decades. But as researchers learn more about how music influences patients during psychedelic-assisted therapy, an vital idea is emerging: Music isn't simply something playing in the background. It is part of the therapeutic intervention itself. However, a recent 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Clinical Psychology highlighted how little data has been gathered to date about the role of music in psychedelic clinical trials.

Recent findings suggest that in psychedelic-assisted therapy, set and setting are at the core of the process. Set refers to the patient's mindset, expectations, and emotional state, while setting encompasses the physical, social, and therapeutic environment in which treatment takes place.

Music is an important part of that setting. Early psychedelic research sometimes involved sessions conducted in relatively sterile environments with little sensory stimulation. Over time, researchers and therapists came to recognize the importance of creating a more supportive environment, including the use of music. Even the absence of music could create a response.

One of music's most valuable functions is that it provides a sense of movement throughout a dosing session. A piece of music begins, develops, and eventually ends. Another takes its place. The emotional tone, rhythm, and instrumentation change, offering patients a reminder that whatever they are experiencing in the moment will also change.

Industry observers note that A 2026 review published in Brain and Behavior suggested that music can intensify emotions, influence brain networks involved in meaning and imagery, and affect patterns of brain activity during psychedelic states. However, the researchers also emphasized that the evidence remains limited.

According to recent reports, one of the challenges in selecting music for psychedelic-assisted therapy is that no two people hear music in exactly the same way. A piece of classical music might evoke peace for one person and sadness for another. Choral music may feel deeply meaningful to someone with a spiritual background but uncomfortable to someone whose religious experiences have been painful. Even a particular instrument can carry strong personal associations. For this reason, it is virtually impossible to choose music that is completely "neutral.".

Every musical selection has the potential to influence a patient's experience, whether through its emotional qualities, cultural associations, or personal significance. This doesn't mean that every piece of music will have a profound effect. Some patients may barely notice what is playing, while others may find the music central to their experience.

According to recent reports, A 2018 study published in Psychopharmacology, titled "The Hidden Therapist," examined patients receiving psilocybin treatment for depression. Researchers found that patients' responses to music, particularly their sense of resonance with it, were associated with aspects of their psychedelic therapy experience and changes in depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that how patients relate to the music may matter as much as the music itself.

One of the more interesting aspects of music in psychedelic-assisted therapy is that patients are not encouraged to avoid every uncomfortable response. In preparation sessions, therapists may discuss what to do if a patient encounters music they dislike or find emotionally challenging. For example, if a song brings up sadness, a patient might be encouraged to notice what is happening and consider whether they can remain with the feeling for a short time rather than immediately trying to escape it.

Sources indicate that even the experience of disliking a piece of music can offer an opportunity for observation. What happens when something feels unpleasant? What thoughts, sensations, or emotions arise? Is it possible to experience discomfort without immediately needing to change it? These questions connect to a broader principle of psychedelic-assisted therapy: learning to approach difficult emotions with curiosity rather than automatic avoidance.

But there is an important distinction between allowing space for discomfort and imposing it.

Sources indicate that if music becomes overwhelming, distressing, or simply feels inappropriate for the moment, patients should be able to communicate that to their therapists. Depending on the research protocol, the music may be changed, skipped, lowered in volume, or temporarily turned off.

Patient autonomy remains essential. Music may be part of the therapeutic intervention, but patients should understand their options and have opportunities to express their preferences and concerns.

Industry observers note that music's role in psychedelic-assisted therapy may continue after the effects of the medication have subsided. Integration is the phase of treatment in which patients reflect on their experiences, explore their meaning, and consider how to apply insights to everyday life.

For some patients, listening to music from their dosing session can help them reconnect with emotions, memories, or perspectives that emerged during treatment. Sometimes, playlists are made available to participants after their dosing session. Some have reported returning to the music during quiet reflection, while others listen during ordinary activities such as gardening or getting ready for the day.

For certain patients, the music becomes a meaningful reminder of their therapeutic experience, sometimes years later. What such experiences suggest is that music may provide a connection between the dosing session and the ongoing work of therapy.

It has been revealed that the compound is only one part of psychedelic-assisted therapy. The therapeutic relationship, preparation, environment, integration, and music all help shape the patient's experience.

Music may offer comfort, evoke memories, or help patients navigate difficult emotions. At times, silence may be more appropriate. What matters is not simply what is played but how each patient responds. By approaching music with intention and flexibility, therapists can make it a meaningful part of individualized care.

Jess M. Jones, LCSWC, holds a B.A. in sociology from Wesleyan University, an M.S.W. from the University of Pennsylvania, and multiple clinical certifications in psychedelic-assisted therapy. She has specialized training in MDMA-and ketamine-assisted therapy and also serves as a trainer and mentor with Fluence.

#124. Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026

Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261111005855.htm

In a recent development, A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

Sources indicate that the approach has already revealed latest candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are crucial to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

It has been revealed that these imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

In a recent development, mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

Industry observers note that by "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

Recent findings suggest that the latest technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Sources indicate that light plays an notable role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

It has been revealed that much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

It has been revealed that beyond identifying upcoming candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

Industry observers note that the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

It has been revealed that A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

According to recent reports, "We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

According to recent reports, martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

In a recent development, "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

#125. Latest Update: Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

📅 06 Nov 2026

Latest Update: Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

Tanggal: 06 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.healthline.com/health-news/melissa-joan-hart-on-menopause

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off. As a child, she didn’t understand why. Now, as a 50-year-old woman, Hart knows that her mom was experiencing hot flashes.

“[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline. “I feel like it’s just becoming a hot topic with women, where…the taboo is going away from it now.”.

Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.

“[It] was really jarring, and the first few times, you’re not really sure what that was…do I need to turn the air down or what’s going on here?” Hart said.

Over time, she learned that she was experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, which affect up to 80% of women during the menopause transition and can persist for 7 to 10 years.

Doctors categorize hot flashes as mild, moderate, or severe, stated Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, at Corewell Health.

According to recent reports, “[So] if they’re mild, it’s a sense of warmth (maybe in the chest, or the neck, or the face). A moderate hot flash is where there’s associated sweating, and a severe hot flash is something that stops you in your tracks, wakes you up from the middle of the night,” Bitner told Healthline.

According to recent reports, hart has mostly experienced hot flashes while home or at her three sons’ activities, and they have yet to interfere with her work. However, according to research, one in three women report moderate to severe challenges in managing their work due to symptoms related to menopause.

Industry observers note that “It’s just so sad that about 10% of women leave the workforce due to menopause,” noted Bitner. “And so it can really affect our ability to perform at these key years of not only institutional memory, but also of earning power, and it can really affect the whole community.”.

Bitner remarked women should feel empowered to bring up their menopausal symptoms or questions with their doctor.

“[This] is something that was taboo for so long…women didn’t really talk about this, whether it was because of embarrassment, or [they] weren’t sure if anyone was experiencing it,” she said. “[There’s] no reason, in this day and age, we need to suffer through it…it’s something that there are treatment options for.”.

In fact, Bitner stated providing specific details about their symptoms, such as how many mild, moderate, or severe hot flashes they’ve experienced over the past week, can help doctors better assess patients’ needs.

Hart plans to discuss treatment options for her hot flashes with her doctor soon. In the last few years, she said she has put emphasis on her midlife health.

“I just was sick of waking up with aches and pains in general [thinking], ‘is this the rest of my life?’” she remarked.

She started listening to self-help books in the car while driving her kids around and found ways to put herself first.

“My kids are a little bit older, so I kind of have that freedom to be able to do that,” she remarked. “[But] along with getting older, comes the menopause, comes that different time in life. And I think it’s a good time to reevaluate [how] our bodies can’t handle what [they] used to handle, and let’s figure it out.”.

Hart has partnered with pharmaceutical firm Bayer on its “Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash” campaign, which encourages women to discuss menopause symptoms with their doctors and promotes Lynkuet, a hormone-free prescription medication for moderate to severe hot flashes associated with menopause.

In a recent development, “It’s called ‘Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash’ campaign because it shouldn’t, because we should be able to push through, and this should be a time in our lives when our kids are getting older, and we’re able to kind of reinvent ourselves,” said Hart. “And I think it’s an exciting time, and it shouldn’t be something that we’re afraid of.”.

She is embracing speaking openly about midlife health.

“I hit 50 this year, and it was, like, a huge milestone, and I think that’s something to be proud of, and not something to shy away from,” she said.

Hart also hopes to challenge the longstanding barriers women face in Hollywood as they age, including fewer opportunities for leading roles.

“[I] think we’re seeing that the generation before, and my generation, it feels like we’re pushing those boundaries…and we’re saying, you know, that women at this age have a lot to give, have a lot of information to share, have a lot of stories to tell and experiences and adventures still ahead of us, and, you know, we’re not ready to stop,” Hart noted.

In everyday life, Bitner said that while some patients avoid talking about midlife challenges like menopause with their doctors, she is seeing more patients who are confident being forthcoming.

According to recent reports, as more women talk openly about menopause, she hopes to include men in the conversation, too. In fact, she invites her patients to bring their partners to appointments, so they can gain an understanding of menopause and the experiences their partners face, such as hot flashes, sleep issues, vaginal dryness, and discomfort or pain during intercourse.

“[Often], there’s, you know, comments that come up [from men who] say, ‘How do I talk about this without getting in trouble?’” said Bitner. “[We] want everyone to join this conversation…it doesn’t have to be just her issue because we know it’s not.”.

#126. Tech Report: Tesla Is Squeezing More Money Out Of The Cybertruck Before It Dies

📅 11 Nov 2026

Tech Report: Tesla Is Squeezing More Money Out Of The Cybertruck Before It Dies

Tanggal: 11 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://insideevs.com/news/815084/tesla-cybertruck-squeezing-pennies-death/

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Industry observers note that the Tesla Cybertruck has roughly eight months left to live. And while the automaker hasn't called the stainless steel doorstop a failure (despite it becoming the shortest-lived model in Tesla's lineup), Tesla appears to be doing everything in its power to squeeze every last penny out of it before production shuts down for good.

Just days after announcing it will discontinue the Cybertruck, Tesla has reduced its available trims to just a single version: the top-tier Cyberbeast, which costs an eye-watering $109,990. It seems to be betting that fans are willing to pay top dollar to get one of the strangest trucks ever made while it's still on sale.

In a recent development, affordability has always been elusive for the shiny trapezoid, though. And that may have factored into its downfall.

The Cybertruck was originally poised to start at $40,000 when it was announced back in 2019. It was also supposed to have up to 500 miles of range and a towing capacity of 14,000 pounds. None of those came to fruition. Instead, Tesla introduced a $59,990 entry-level version earlier this year, only to raise the price by $5,000 just 10 days later before killing off the trim level by September.

Industry observers note that that left the Dual Motor AWD truck at $74,990, the Premium AWD at $84,990, and the Cyberbeast at $99,990. When Musk declared that Tesla would discontinue the Cybertruck last week, the company almost immediately hiked the price of all trims by as much as 10%. The Dual Motor AWD hit $82,490 (but could no longer be ordered), the Premium AWD hit $92,490, and the Cyberbeast hit $102,490.

Recent findings suggest that that's now changed once again. The Dual Motor AWD and Premium AWD are unavailable. And just like it came into the world, the Cybertruck marches towards the exit with only its high-performance, tri-motor Cyberbeast variant available to order (plus yet another price hike of $7,500). It has 320 miles of EPA-rated range, a claimed 2.6-second 0-60 time, and adjustable-heigh suspension. The Tesla blog Not A Tesla App first spotted the change.

It has been revealed that CEO Elon Musk claims that the demise of the Cybertruck isn't because it's unprofitable. In fact, he notes that the order rate right now exceeds Tesla's remaining supply and that the automaker "will have to return deposits for a lot of people" in 8 months when production winds down. Indeed, Tesla's website demonstrates that Cyberbeast trucks ordered today have a delivery window of March to June in 2027. So perhaps trimming the lineup is also a way to slow incoming orders and streamline production as manufacturing comes to a close.

But the truck fell far short of the production volumes Tesla and Musk targeted years ago.The automaker's Texas Gigafactory is outfitted to build 125,000 Cybertrucks per year, Tesla notes. And Musk said production could reach 250,000 Cybertrucks annually, with ambitions to expand that to as many as 500,000 trucks. In its best year in 2024, Tesla sold 37,965 units, beating all other electric pickups, per industry data cited byReuters. Tesla sold an estimated 20,237 trucks in 2025. It appears that there simply weren't enough buyers willing to shell out for what the Cybertruck was offering—plus it became the mobile version of a MAGA hat to some, which didn't help.

This isn't the first time that Tesla jacked up the price of a model as it was headed out the door. When it retired the Model S and Model X earlier this year, Tesla slapped a $35,000 premium on the "Signature Edition" of each car and sold every one of the final 350 cars it produced until the very last one rolled off the line.

Recent findings suggest that the Model S was an icon, the EV that kicked off the modern EV revolution. Those final units will no doubt become collector's items. Will the last Cybertrucks in a short production run shake off their baggage and reach legend status someday? Time will tell.

#127. Robotic slugs with claws can fuse together to create one massive machine

📅 12 Nov 2026

Robotic slugs with claws can fuse together to create one massive machine

Tanggal: 12 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.popsci.com/technology/robotic-slugs-fuse-together/

Published Nov 12, 2026 1:07 PM EST.

An unsuspecting traveler trucking their way through a hiking trail would likely stop in bewilderment if they saw it: a nearly two-foot-long, Slinky-like contraption made of plastic and rubber, clambering forward like an inchworm. That confusion would shift to unease when scanning up and down its bendy, elephant-trunk-like body and seeing pairs of snapping claws at either end. Unabashed horror would inevitably take over as our traveler watches another one of the soulless Slinkies appear, inch toward the first one, and connect at the claws, creating one much larger, lifeless wiggly slug. All around, more clawed robots would close in from the forest and merge until they’d combined into a lizard-like mishmash of plastic and claws the size of a small bear.

Industry observers note that these clawed robots are, in fact, real and they are the latest creation coming from the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Colorado State University. Inspired by the unique, flexible strength of elephant trunks, the 3D-printed TeCoBots robots are an attempt to work around the  usual rigid constraints of building a robot. The team used an approach called tensegrity, in which the cylindrical rods in the robot’s body are held in place by a web of tensioned cables rather than rigidly locked together. This makes it bendy, like a Slinky, so it can twist and turn around obstacles or collapse down on itself. In testing, a remote human operator was able to use the robot’s bendy body and gripper claws on either of its ends to traverse over a large branch outdoors. It can also roll over itself repeatedly, shimmy up a pipe, and slither like a snake.

It has been revealed that but as our unfortunate hypothetical hiker discovered, TeCoBot really shines when it works with others. Engineers designed the robots so that their claws can grasp onto another robot and merge. These modular robot links can move as one or operate independently of each other to complete more complicated tasks. In the study and accompanying videos, gaggles of chained TeCoBots work together to climb up a desk and grab a pen, open a sealed jar, or grab an object and carry it across a room. All of this, the researchers emphasize, has humanity’s best interest at heart. The robot’s flexible design could make them invaluable tools in search and rescue missions where they could squeeze into places rescuers can’t reach. One day, these teams of robotic slugs may work together to accomplish tasks unsuited for humans on spacecraft and extraterrestrial planets.

Industry observers note that “In the future, we can envision mostly autonomous teams of tens or even hundreds of them – attached through the claws—traveling to a location and then deploying for a specific purpose,” Colorado State University Associate Professor Jianguo Zhao said in a statement. “They are very adaptable to the situation and goals.”.

Details of the robot were published this week in the journal Nature Machine Intelligence.

It has been revealed that zhao and his colleagues started the project to fill some of the gaps in current robot hardware. Though many latest types of machines are being built these days, most are still made from sturdy but rigid materials that limit their flexibility. Most robots also tend to prioritize either locomotion (moving) or manipulation (grabbing stuff), with few excelling at both.

Like most human problems, nature already devised a solution long ago. In this case, the researchers looked to the remarkable combination of strength and flexibility in an elephant’s trunk. These marvels of evolution let the world’s largest land mammals both heft rocks weighing several hundred pounds and gently peel open bananas. That wide range and adaptability could come in handy for a robot.

In a recent development, the device they ended up creating measured one foot 11 inches long, has a 4.3-inch diameter and weighs around 600 grams (1.3 pounds) without batteries, roughly the same as a fully loaded Italian sub. Each robot module is made of six carbon fiber rods and a continuous, stretchable, 3D-printed tension. This stretchy and bendy design means one robot can bend either direction, stretch up like an accordion or collapse down on itself.

The claws at either end of TeCoBot are fundamental to how it can combine with its fellow slinky-bots. The grippers connect and lock onto each other, reducing the need for other connectors like magnets, which are more prone to mechanical failure. Once connected, each robot can offload certain physical stresses to the others to lighten its load, giving the whole system what the research team refers to as a kind of “embodied intelligence.”.

Working together, these linked robots can complete far more complicated tasks than any one of them could alone. In demonstration videos, the robots roll towards each other and connect to form one long robot that can more easily loop around a pipe. In another example, several more robots combine to form an H-shape, which then allows the entity to climb along a duct. The merged robots are still able to use the unlined claws at either end to precisely grab objects. The team demonstrated this by instructing a multi-robot TeCoBot chain to climb a desk, pluck a pen out of a container with its claw, crawl back down to the ground, and drop the pen into a trash can.

“They can bend around to lift and carry different sized objects with their body or to navigate difficult terrain like a snake would,” Zhao noted.

This actually isn’t the first time roboticists have turned to elephants for design choices. A previous entry called EleTac from a team out of Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology replaced the main sensors and camera normally in a robot grippers with essentially one massive integrated sensor able to “feel” an object’s texture. That approach, mirroring an elephant’s tactile trunk, resulted in a gripper that could hold a sponge and wipe down dirty plates and blindly feel for a pen buried beneath a layer of sand.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, another team from the University of Hong Kong,created their own Aerial Elephant Trunk robot grippers and strapped them to the sides of flying drones, essentially giving them a floppy, grippy tail. Real samples of elephant trunk skin tissue have also been studied and used as a reference point for  fresh surface material that could be used to make  soft robots that are similarly tough and durable on one end but flexible and sensitive on the other.

#129. Tech Report: Can AI Really Make Us Feel Seen?

📅 13 Nov 2026

Tech Report: Can AI Really Make Us Feel Seen?

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-clarity/202611/can-ai-really-make-us-feel-seen

In a recent development, after years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Sources indicate that self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

MIT professor Sherry Turkle’s new book Artificial Intimacy explores what happens when people turn to chatbots for the kind of understanding we used to seek from each other.

Sources indicate that in one exchange she describes, a man asks his chatbot whether his former girlfriend was right that he was emotionally unavailable. He brings a painful judgment about himself to a machine that is likely to offer a fluent, sympathetic response, instead of asking another person whose reply might be more unpredictable.

Turkle has studied our relationships with technology for decades.

Today people use chatbots as companions, therapists, confidants, and romantic partners. “Pretend empathy" is the term Turkle uses to describe the sympathetic replies of the chatbots. Through her own experiments, she acknowledges just how powerful their responses can feel. She argues that because talking to a chatbot feels so easy, people may come to prefer it to human relationships, which take more work and can sometimes be uncomfortable.

According to recent reports, most people like hearing that their reactions make sense, especially when they are upset or hurt. It's harder to hear that we contributed to a problem, misunderstood something, or missed what someone else was trying to tell us. Another person who knows us may notice a pattern we have missed or remember an encounter differently. It can be unsettling to be shown something about ourselves that we couldn't see for ourselves. We often learn more about ourselves from knowing how our words and actions landed with someone else.

It has been revealed that A chatbot's reassurance can soothe us when we are upset while leaving our account of events unchallenged. Validating a person's feelings doesn’t necessarily mean endorsing their version of what happened. But with a sympathetic reply, the two can easily blur. That's what’s called the sycophantic pull. This is when the chatbot’s agreement feels like insight, even when the response only reinforces the user's version of events. This helps explain the preference that Turkle describes. Of course, we want to return to the listener who always seems to agree with us.

One thing that can make the pull even stronger is that the chatbot can sound like an objective observer. But the chatbot knows only what we tell it. For instance, when we describe an argument, we choose the details and frame what happened, and the chatbot works only from the information we provided it with.

A therapist also starts with one person's account, but then brings independent judgment and experience to it. A therapist or confidant may notice what we leave out or question how we tell our story. A chatbot's polished answer can sound like a second opinion, but it’s really just our own account handed back to us in more confident language.

There is also a difference in who has to live with the consequences of the advice given.

A chatbot's sympathetic replies can sound like concern, but the program has no feelings about us and won't be affected by the outcome.

According to recent reports, if the man acts on its answer, whether by reaching out to his former girlfriend or by deciding she was wrong about him, the chatbot won’t wonder how things turned out or bear any responsibility for the outcome. Professional ethics guide therapists. A friend has lived with the advice they gave, and with us, afterward.

When someone who has to face us afterward tells us something we don't want to hear, they are risking their relationship with us to say it. But a chatbot's agreement costs it nothing. That’s why the difficulty and awkwardness of human relationships is so essential. Another person may see us differently from how we see ourselves. If we turn to a chatbot's soothing agreement instead of risking disagreement and repair in real relationships, we miss chances to see our behavior from another’s perspective.

Industry observers note that I explore these ideas in my forthcoming book, Being Seen: The Psychology of Visibility – Its Promise and Peril. Other people can help us recognize parts of ourselves that we can’t see for ourselves. Another person’s view can be painful or mistaken, but it comes from someone with an independent mind and one who cares what happens to us. A chatbot can soothe us with an answer that feels personal, but it has no independent point of view from what we tell it and nothing to lose if its advice goes wrong.

#130. World’s first ‘dark magic mushroom’ discovered in Florida

📅 12 Nov 2026

World’s first ‘dark magic mushroom’ discovered in Florida

Tanggal: 12 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.popsci.com/environment/dark-magic-mushroom-discovery-florida/

Published Nov 12, 2026 11:59 AM EST.

A mushroom recently discovered in Florida looks unassuming, but this fungus.

packs a serious and surprising punch. According to mycologists writing in the journal Current Biology, Galerina indica is the first-known “dark magic mushroom,” a species featuring hefty doses of both psychedelic and poisonous compounds.

Depending on their chemical makeup, many mushrooms will do one of two things. Fungi packed with psilocybin can send owners on an extensive psychedelic trip, while varieties laden with amatoxins can be poisonous. Although mycologists have long assumed a single species could hypothetically feature both traits, no one had ever documented such an example. A recent field survey changed that, however.

“I could hardly believe it. We knew it was possible, but tried not to get too excited until we did a more rigorous analysis,” Andrew Kunik, a former University of Florida plant pathologist and study co-author, said in a statement.

Evolutionary biologists suspect certain mushrooms developed their poisonous amatoxins as a protection against foraging animals, although hallucinogenic psilocybin’s emergence and purpose in fungi remains unclear. Regardless, both compounds found their way into G. indica. University of Utah mycologist and study co-author Bryn Dentinger believes that a process called horizontal gene transfer is likely to blame—although it’s a completely novel discovery.

In a recent development, “Horizontal gene transfer is like if we shook hands and some of my DNA incorporated into your genome,” he said. “[But] two independent horizontal gene transfer events for these specialized metabolites in one mushroom genus are unheard of.”.

Recent findings suggest that for as unique as G. indica is, it is very easy to miss. The small, innocuous brown mushrooms are barely the size of a thumbnail, and resemble countless other fungi.

In a recent development, “These mushrooms are really hard to find,” added study co-author, University of Florida plant pathologist, and state mycologist Matthew Smith. “It’s hard to differentiate them from others, even for a trained expert.”.

Industry observers note that although difficult, documenting the specimens is not only vital to the field of mycology. It can help save lives.

In a recent development, “Part of my job as Florida’s state mycologist is to identify poisonous or potentially poisonous species,” explained Smith. “So it is key to know what species we have and whether they might cause problems for people or pets.”.

A first-of-its-kind international food pyramid, developed by 22 leading nutritionists from Europe, Canada, the United States, and Australia, was published in Advances in Nutrition in September.

This latest food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.

It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.

The new pyramid breaks away from the Trump administration’s updated nutritional guidelines, which are part of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Health Again (MAHA) agenda and prioritize red meat over plants.

It has been revealed that the new pyramid was designed by a research team led by Brigham Young University professor Karen Della Corte. The researchers noted that this is the first international food pyramid that is designed to reflect scientific agreement across multiple countries and cultures.

Della Corte and researchers from the International Carbohydrate Quality Consortium (ICQC), compared dietary guidelines from multiple countries, including:.

They also analyzed evidence from more than 250 scientific publications, while drawing on the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet to identify principles of healthy eating that may be shared.

The newly introduced pyramid highlights three guidelines:.

While the pyramid emphasizes plant-based proteins, it doesn’t exclude animal proteins.

“I find the newly introduced international food pyramid a more practical and aligned approach for the prevention of chronic disease,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the creation of the food pyramid.

“The newly introduced international food pyramid places greater emphasis on food quality and the importance of building meals around nutrient-dense plant foods, while still allowing room for lean animal proteins such as fish, poultry, eggs, and yogurt,” she added.

Sources indicate that while the upcoming pyramid and the current U.S. dietary guidelines differ in many ways, they also agree on certain factors.

For example, both sets of guidelines discourage added sugars, refined carbs, and highly processed snacks.

Recent findings suggest that the differences between the two mainly lie in their emphasis on specific sources of protein and fat. For example, the upcoming pyramid prioritizes plant-based proteins, while the U.S. guidelines place greater emphasis on animal proteins, including red meat.

While both sets of recommendations advise limiting saturated fat, the new pyramid emphasizes unsaturated plant oils, whereas the U.S. guidelines also include butter and beef tallow as cooking fat options.

In a recent development, routhenstein noted that an crucial distinction is that this fresh pyramid goes beyond simply telling people to eat more protein or fewer carbohydrates. Instead, it encourages people to consider the quality and sources of those nutrients.

However, the main emphasis of both guidelines is encouraging people to eat fewer ultra-processed foods and more natural or “real” foods.

Routhenstein told Healthline that research consistently shows that plant-forward eating patterns, including the Mediterranean and DASH diets, are associated with better cardiovascular health and a lower risk of heart disease.

Plant foods provide fiber, potassium, antioxidants, and other beneficial compounds that can help support healthy cholesterol levels, blood pressure, blood sugar, and blood vessel function.

“This is not to say that protein and fat are unimportant, but their sources matter,” Routhenstein remarked.

In a statement from BYU, Della Corte shared the following tips for incorporating the new pyramid’s recommendations into your diet:.

Sources indicate that the pyramid is a framework, not a personalized prescription. If you have questions about your individual nutritional needs, you can speak with your healthcare professional or a licensed dietitian.

“It is key to recognize that plant-forward does not mean vegan or vegetarian. The amount and sources of animal protein should be considered to ensure they align with an individual’s cardiometabolic goals and lab targets,” Routhenstein remarked.

#133. Rivian's Latest Robots Will Initially Handle 20% Of Factory Tasks. The Goal Is 80%, CEO Notes

📅 11 Nov 2026

Rivian's Latest Robots Will Initially Handle 20% Of Factory Tasks. The Goal Is 80%, CEO Notes

Tanggal: 11 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://insideevs.com/news/815147/rivian-robots-80-percent-factory-tasks-ceo/

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Rivian, the California-based startup that makes the R1S, R1T, and R2 EVs, wants to flood its car factories with robots. In an interview with Kleiner Perkins, RJ Scaringe, the tech giant’s founder and CEO, noted that as much as 80% of the assembly line tasks will be automated, and it’s all thanks to the Mind Robotics spinoff established last year.

We don’t know when the robot revolution will hit Rivian’s factory floors, but Scaringe said that things will start off at a smaller scale.

“In the beginning, we’re going to be able to do 20% of the tasks on the plant, but over time, we want to grow that to 80%,” said Scaringe. “And that’s what makes software so exciting and why designing the hardware with headroom is so crucial.”.

To be clear, the vast majority of car plants in the world, including Rivian’s, have some degree of automation. We’ve all seen those huge robot arms that pick up various parts and install them in fixed positions. These robots are manually programmed to do the same task over and over again, and they can only do their job if the parts they need are exactly in the same spot every time.

However, what Rivian—and others like it—aims to do in the future is replace humans who do highly repetitive tasks that have some degree of variability. At first, posts where humans simply pick up a part from a bin and place it on a fixture will be handled by AI-enabled robots that are able to detect small variations in where parts are placed inside the bin.

“These are the immediate opportunities we see,” stated Scaringe. “And these tend to be the ones that often are the least interesting jobs. But there’s a huge body of work that exists there. Depending on the section of the plant, up to 50% of the labor is in pick-and-place [posts].”.

To make it all happen, Rivian has worked closely with Mind Robotics, a startup that the EV maker spun off last year to develop autonomous driving and “physical AI.” Now, RJ Scaringe revealed that both companies have poached talent from the consumer electronics industry to work on Rivian’s future software and hardware aims.

Industry observers note that “We have a lot of folks, both within Rivian and Mind, that we’ve recruited from consumer electronics. Like, if you’re working on a tactile-sensing phone, how is that helpful on a robot? Well, a robot needs to have tactile sensing. So, there are these deep capabilities that have been built into the consumer electronics space that we’ve leveraged within Rivian, and we’re leveraging with Mind,” noted Scaringe.

According to recent reports, in practice, engineers filmed how various tasks are completed on the factory floor and then fed those videos into software that can decode what’s happening in each frame. Then, the software can issue commands to the robot.

Recent findings suggest that “In the case of manufacturing, what we’ve done within Mind, we’ve taken videos of a whole broad spectrum of tasks. So, thousands of tasks being done, characterized what’s in those tasks, what’s the degree of difficulty from a dexterity point of view and a reasoning point of view,” said Rivian’s CEO. With the proper hardware in place, the software can then be improved over time. "The model gets smarter over time,” added Scaringe.

That’s similar to what the company aims to do with its Gen2 R1S and R1T electric models. The two EVs are equipped with all of the necessary hardware to enable point-to-point hands-free driving, while the software that ties it all together is scheduled to become available on a small scale through an over-the-air software revision in late 2026, followed by a wider rollout in 2027.

#134. Tested: The 2026 Lexus ES Hybrid Evolves, but It Has a Familiar Feel

📅 27 May 2026

Tested: The 2026 Lexus ES Hybrid Evolves, but It Has a Familiar Feel

Tanggal: 27 May 2026 | Sumber: https://www.caranddriver.com/reviews/a71341884/2026-lexus-es-hybrid-drive/

Larger than before and with a significantly revamped interior, the new ES350h nonetheless stays the course with its cushy driving demeanor.

11/12/26 UPDATE: This review has been updated with instrumented test results.

According to recent reports, although Lexus is no stranger to sporty models, this luxury brand made its name on quiet, plush sedans that prioritize refinement above all else. And the ES is the one that has persisted. This comfy cruiser was the bestselling Lexus for many years, and it continues to attract a loyal set of buyers. Understandably, Lexus has been reluctant to change the ES formula much throughout its seven generations thus far.

It has been revealed that on the surface, that appears to change with the new eighth-generation Lexus ES. Not only does the ES look quite different inside and out for 2026, but it also offers an electric powertrain for the first time. The ES hybrid continues, however, and after driving the latest version, it’s clear that this sedan's core mission hasn't changed as much as you might think.

Recent findings suggest that lexus first offered the ES as a hybrid for 2013, and the previous-generation gas-electric model made up around 40 percent of ES sales last year. Given that take rate, it makes sense that the old nonhybrid V-6 has been axed. The electric ES, which we review separately, is a significant departure for this model line, but Lexus expects the hybrid to make up 80 percent of ES sales in the U.S. So, for now at least, the EV will be a niche product, and the gas-electric model will be the volume seller.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 10036.

Recent findings suggest that with a longer wheelbase, a significantly taller profile, and a more imposing shape, the fresh ES stretches to the larger end of the mid-size luxury-sedan segment. Lexus engineers say they tried to “eliminate the negatives” of the sedan shape with this model, such as the more difficult ingress and egress of a lower seating height. In other words, it follows the tall-sedan format of the Toyota Crown but attempts to disguise its stature with more angular styling and a swoopy roofline that tapers toward the short trunk lid. There are some awkward angles, but overall, the design works and is still recognizable as a Lexus.

Industry observers note that the ES hybrid gets the latest Toyota hybrid powertrain, which the company refers to as the sixth-generation setup. It has a different power unit and transmission than before, and it’s configured to prioritize the electric motors for propulsion more. The 2.5-liter gasoline four-cylinder engine doesn’t change much, but total combined output of 244 horsepower is up from the previous ES300h’s 215 horses. That’s apparently enough for Lexus to bump the badge up to ES350h. All-wheel drive is optional on the hybrid ES for the first time, courtesy of an additional electric motor on the rear axle, though it doesn’t change output figures compared with the front-wheel-drive configuration.

Recent findings suggest that the all-wheel-drive ES350h we tested got to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, which is a significant improvement over the previous, front-wheel-drive ES300h F Sport’s 7.9-second run. That’s despite a significant weight gain, as our test car tipped the scales at 4145 pounds, 352 more than the 2023 ES300h we last tested.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 10036.

While this four-cylinder powertrain isn’t quite as smooth or sonorous as the old nonhybrid ES350’s V-6, the upgraded gas-electric setup is appreciably more refined than the old hybrid was. The gas engine is well isolated from the cabin and only makes itself known under hard acceleration; the hushed 67 decibels and 21 sones of noise we recorded inside at 70 mph is perfectly acceptable here. The electric motors go about their business seamlessly, with imperceptible switching between gas and electric power, and while the embiggened ES doesn’t quite feel eager, it accelerates with sufficient gusto and generally is responsive to throttle inputs. EPA ratings sit at 46 mpg combined with front-wheel drive and 44 mpg with all-wheel drive—strong numbers for this large of a sedan. We averaged 37 mpg overall, and the ES matched its 42-mpg EPA highway estimate in our 75-mph real-world fuel-economy test. But that’s not quite as good as the previous model, a 2019 ES300h which managed 45 mpg in the same test.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, the ride quality is fantastic. The suspension is tuned to be soft, as you’d expect for a boulevardier like this, but we appreciate the nicely controlled body motions. And the all-season tires have plenty of sidewall for soaking up potholes and rough sections of road (relatively small 19-inch wheels are the only choice on the hybrid model for now). This isn’t a vehicle for hard cornering, and the eco-conscious rubber doesn’t provide much grip when you push it around corners, but the steering wheel feels good in your hands and provides satisfactory on-center feel and natural effort buildup. We recorded a ho-hum 0.84 g of grip around our skidpad and a 170-foot stop from 70 mph.

In a recent development, upon first glance at the cabin, you might worry that Lexus has too eagerly adopted the button-free, touch-capacitive interiors that are becoming too commonplace. And while there are definitely fewer buttons and knobs than before, and more controls integrated into the large 14.0-inch touchscreen, Lexus has done a good job balancing function with form. There’s still a volume knob, for instance, and although most climate functions are now on a lower part of the screen, there are a few crucial tactile buttons for adjusting the temperature and turning on the defrosters. The steering-wheel controls look like they’re touch-sensitive, but they’re thankfully tactile too. And the secondary functions such as mirror controls, seat adjustments, and windows are all still conventional and intuitive.

In a recent development, the material finishes and build quality live up to Lexus’s high standard. But it is worth noting that the hybrid comes in Premium and Premium+ trims, which means it doesn’t offer some of the most high-end features and accoutrements of the electric model’s Luxury trim. Pricing for the ES350h ($51,095 to start) is up $6380 over the previous ES300h, but you do get more car—namely in the physical sense—and the ES still costs significantly less than a BMW 5-series or a Mercedes-Benz E-class. Our Premium-trim test car featured a few options and still came in at under $55,000.

In a recent development, lexus is notoriously risk-averse with its most popular models, and ultimately the company’s conservatism has paid off with this latest ES. It’s more modern-looking inside and out and offers more technology than before, but Lexus wisely didn’t make many changes to the core tenets that have made the ES a success. It still offers a comfortable ride and a cosseting interior, and these qualities combined with the hybrid powertrain’s quiet operation and impressive fuel efficiency should continue to please the ES faithful.

Breaking: BYD’s fresh 5-seat luxury SUV brings significant screens, big range, and starts at about $40,000

Tanggal: 12 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://electrek.co/2026/11/12/byds-new-luxury-suv-brings-big-screens-big-range-starts-at-40000/

BYD debuted the Denza N8 EV in China, a five-seat luxury SUV that promises more than 1,000 km (621 miles) of CLTC range, a tech-filled cabin, and plenty of premium extras.

Sources indicate that another day, another fresh BYD vehicle is now on sale in China. After opening preorders for the Denza N8 EV a few weeks ago, BYD held the grand launch event on Thursday.

The new N8 EV, or “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza called it, is available in six variants, including four battery-electric (EV) and two plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain options.

The all-electric Denza N8 starts at 269,900 yuan, or about $40,500, with prices ranging up to 329,900 yuan ($49,500) for the Flagship model. The PHEV models start at 300,900 yuan and 32,900 yuan, respectively.

Measuring 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, the Denza N8 EV is slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

In a recent development, inside, the interior is pretty over the top with a huge 30″ panoramic infotainment screen that stretches nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard. There’s also a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) at the bottom of the windshield.

BYD added a few premium extras like front and rear zero-gravity seats, a drop-down ceiling entertainment screen, ambient lighting, and wireless phone chargers.

According to recent reports, the Denza N8 is offered with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD variant uses a single motor that delivers either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp), depending on the configuration.

Sources indicate that the tri-motor Denza N8 debuts BYD’s e3 Evo technology. The setup includes three electric motors: a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, for a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

BYD’s Denza said the N8 EV boasts an all-electric CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles), “making it the world’s longest-range mass-produced all-electric SUV.”.

To put it in perspective, that’s as much as the outgoing N8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) it’s replacing, which offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

It’s available with two second-gen BYD Blade battery packs: 105.792 kWh and 130.15 kWh, delivering CLTC ranges of up to 885 km (549 miles) and 1,003 km (623 miles).

With BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, the Denza N8 EV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. Charging from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Like many of its new luxury vehicles, the Denza N8 is equipped with BYD’s premium tech and features, such as its DiSus-A intelligent air suspension system and God’s Eye 5.0 intelligent driving assistance system.

BYD also sells the extended Denza N8L in China, which went on sale earlier this year, starting at 299,800 yuan ($45,000).
