Exploring the great outdoors is all about preparedness—and the Blue Oval’s latest Expedition build is ready for just about anything.

Overlanding doesn’t exactly come with a fixed set of rules. As long as the vehicle makes it off the trail at the end of the journey, whether it’s after an hour or a year, the mission has been accomplished—and Ford’s latest Expedition build is designed to stay out and make the most of the great outdoors in a way real overlanders can get behind.

It has been revealed that the new rig, officially known as the Project Overland Expedition Tremor, pushes Dearborn’s full-size SUV to its off-road limit. Sadly, Ford specified that this project vehicle would not be sold to the public, but we’d sure like to take this special Expedition Tremor deep into the woods.

#197. Latest Update: Unblending: the IFS Approach to Learning

📅 13 Nov 2026

Latest Update: Unblending: the IFS Approach to Learning

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/internal-family-systems-therapy-for-shame-and-guilt/202611/unblending-the-ifs-approach-to

It has been revealed that after years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Sources indicate that self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Recent findings suggest that artists, writers, and musicians shape experience and hold the interest of an audience by introducing things that are unresolved, promise resolution, and offer hints along the way. A crime novel asks whodunnit; music creates gripping tension and aesthetic chills; plays and movies pose and ponder problems; paintings invite, and so on. Artists know that we stay with what we do not yet understand and we feel thrilled at discovery.

The journey from not knowing to understanding by way of curiosity and exploration is called an epistemic arc. Sometimes we’re captured by a puzzle and we understand gradually, sometimes the epiphany comes quickly. In either case, that aha! moment signifies the soft thump of the tiny dopamine hit that culminates an exploration. But to reach this moment, we have to be open to our existing ideas about identity and relationships being incomplete.

From the Internal Family Systems (IFS) perspective, we all have parts. We may see, hear, sense, or feel them. They present at different ages and, often, act in ways that don’t fit the current moment because they’re stuck in the past. When a part takes over and we see the world through its eyes, expecting what it expects, IFS says the part is blended. This can cause epochal (and often epical) cognitive confusion. Who am I? How old am I? Why do I think this way, feel this way, act this way? In contrast, when the part separates, or unblends, we can notice and relate to it. When we pay attention, parts unblend and we can get into relationship with them, ask what they fear, and meet their need for validation, connection, and love.

Sources indicate that IFS therapy sessions follow the epistemic arc. Clients arrive in therapy puzzled by their behavior (Why do I pull away when I want connection?), but wedded to some familiar certainty, like I am bad, or no one can be trusted. The IFS inquiry invites them to be curious about their behavior and beliefs, which almost always leads to formative experiences.

According to recent reports, the phenomena IFS calls blending and unblending illustrate a paradox at the heart of subjective experience. We can be a part or we can be with a part. When we are a part, we think, feel, and act like that part, but when we are with a part, we have choices. If, for example, a blended part expects rejection, we are likely to hear silence as rejection and view a later offer of help as untrustworthy or dangerous. The part is too afraid to try something latest and our present remains a perpetual repetition of the past. But the opposite is true as well. If the part unblends and we are with it, we can explore its fear and challenge distorted and inaccurate beliefs. I can feel and hear a part that expects to be rejected, but since I’ll be okay whatever happens, I can afford to try something new.

According to recent reports, an IFS session follows an epistemic arc, a process we can understand through the lens of neuroscience and predictive processing, which indicates the brain builds a world model in childhood and then, conserving energy, predicts the familiar. Ideally, the brain updates its predictive model in response to prediction errors, but fear and negative identity beliefs can get in the way. A person who expects rejection and withdraws will not get a chance to learn how others might respond if they were to stay present and express a need.

In a recent development, from the predictive processing perspective, blended parts block the brain’s ability to learn. In contrast, unblending clears the runway. IFS aims to persuade parts to unblend. Our compassion and respect invite engagement, parts acknowledge us, and mutual curiosity sustains investigation. Once parts feel valid, legitimate, lovable, and connected, we feel—and are—more open to experiences that disconfirm old beliefs. Expectations relax, other information gains influence, and the brain’s world model updates.

According to recent reports, an IFS inquiry doesn’t push for change. Pressing a part to step aside or move swiftly can confirm an expectation that its wishes and limits will be disregarded. Patience conveys concern and respect, and is valuable in itself. The message to parts is: You can hesitate and stay connected. You can express fear and be heard. IFS invites all parts to take time exploring their fears and needs. Faster? Slower? You’re the boss.

In a recent development, if you want to discover the logic behind some apparently inexplicable behavior of your own, encourage your parts to unblend. Try noticing them and getting curious. You might have a protective part that keeps everyone happy because it expects disagreements to end relationships. Or you might have a part that withdraws because it anticipates unreasonable—or unmeetable—demands. Your protectors can explain the rationale for their beliefs and behaviors. Your job is to listen with an open heart.

According to recent reports, as you listen, you can validate protective choices but also challenge negative identity conclusions (I’m worthless… something is wrong with me). You can offer to replace old survival tactics with better options. You don’t have to undo the past, convince transgressors to take it back, or prove your worth. The part you protect is valid, lovable, and—if you let me help—loved. Your protectors may need to move toward this invitation slowly, starting with a question they can now tolerate asking: Can things be different? But those aha! moments, when they come, are transformative.

Industry observers note that schwartz, R.C. & Sweezy, M. (2020). Internal Family Systems Therapy (2nd ed.). New York NY: Guilford Press.

#198. Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026

Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

Tanggal: 11 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://electrek.co/2026/11/11/tesla-semi-delivery-50-trucks-chicago-hmd/

Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

It’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its newly introduced Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

Sources indicate that but the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

HMD took its first truck on November 2 and claims it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler said Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

Sources indicate that the company ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

Owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

Industry observers note that tesla introduced volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It indicates the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

So we’re left with proxies. Tesla indicates its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how substantial that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

Sources indicate that the order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

In a recent development, tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that shows whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

Recent findings suggest that I think the semi is going to be a massive seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

In a recent development, our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. #199. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Tanggal: 01 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.healthline.com/health-news/leading-medical-groups-redefine-female-cardiovascular-health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

In a recent development, they stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

According to recent reports, the authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” stated Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she remarked.

“I am incredibly excited to see these latest reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah noted.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is crucial, especially for risk reduction.

Sources indicate that she noted issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” mentioned Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are important windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” remarked William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

According to recent reports, the authors note several age-related warning signs of heart problems. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Sources indicate that females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” remarked Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they noted could reverse these trends. Among them:.

It has been revealed that experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She remarked that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Sources indicate that khan said women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

#200. College student develops LEGO-like, 3D-printed moon bricks

📅 10 Nov 2026

College student develops LEGO-like, 3D-printed moon bricks

Tanggal: 10 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.popsci.com/science/3d-printed-lunar-lego-bricks/

Published Nov 10, 2026 4:30 PM EST.

A permanent lunar base will require structures resilient enough to withstand everything from cosmic radiation and micro-meteorites to moonquakes. There are plenty of building materials to choose from on Earth, but they all come with a catch: transportation storage aboard spacecraft is limited, and each additional pound of cargo will promptly ramp up costs. Engineers have spent years experimenting with ways for future astronauts to source local lunar ingredients, including fine moon dust known as regolith. Unfortunately, most require various binding ingredients that must still be sent from back home.

A college student at the University of Arkansas (U of A) recently had a different idea. In a collaboration with U of A mechanical engineer Wan Shou, Cole McCallum harnessed a specialized method of 3D printing to manufacture LEGO-esque bricks from lunar dust, no binding required. (These aren’t to be confused with LEGO’s actual lunar bricks mockups). Their results published in the journal NPJ Advanced Manufacturing indicate the bricks could be a promising material to investigate as humanity readies itself for a return to the moon.

Lunar regolith is a tricky material. Unlike Earth’s dirt, it doesn’t contain any amount of organic matter. It’s just loose, sharp-edged particles generated by billions’ of years of asteroid and meteor impacts. This means that moon dust can’t bind on its own and requires at least some secondary ingredients.

It has been revealed that while an undergraduate at the U of A, McCallum wondered if a specific type of 3D printing called laser powder bed fusion could offer a workaround. In this technique, fine powder is placed on a flat bed, then exposed to a highly powerful laser beam that fuses each microscopic particle together in a process called sintering. The tray bed lowers down to allow another layer of sintered powder, then repeats the steps until a single, solid block is created. Regolith fits the mold perfectly, so to speak.

“There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum remarked in a university profile.

McCallum and Shou didn’t have access to actual lunar material, so they obtained Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercial material that replicates the moon dust collected by Apollo astronauts during the 1960s and 70s. They ultimately settled on two shapes, one that resembles a cross and another that looks like the letter “H.” The researchers then 3D-printed tiny prototypes measuring a few centimeters wide that they could connect like LEGOs to construct larger structures.

There are still some important caveats to this sintered regolith strategy. McCallum’s blocks are much more porous and weaker than materials containing binders. Additional research is needed to see how the approach works in a vacuum or microgravity, two inescapable hurdles to living on the moon.

According to recent reports, “These structures we’re making can be self-supported. But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet,” said McCallum.

That remarked, his demonstration that even a basic framework for lunar base bricks is achievable solely with regolith may offer a promising direction for mission engineers.

#202. Meta's Billions Won't Fix Youth Mental Health on Its Own

📅 13 Nov 2026

Meta's Billions Won't Fix Youth Mental Health on Its Own

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-game-changers/202611/metas-billions-wont-fix-youth-mental-health-on-its-own

It has been revealed that after years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

It has been revealed that self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

If I had $17 billion dollars from Meta in the settlement of one social media addiction case, I know exactly what I would not do with it. I would not spend it the way states have been spending their opioid settlement money.

Over the past several years, tens of billions of dollars have flowed to states from opioid settlements meant to save lives through prevention, treatment, and recovery. While opioid-related deaths have declined, how much of that decline is attributable to settlement-funded initiatives is unclear. This is a fact researchers partly trace to the glacial pace of spending, fragmented efforts, and a lack of transparency.

Now, states face a smaller-scale version of the same test, this time over youth and social media. In late August, Meta agreed to pay $12.1 billion to resolve a lawsuit brought by 47 states and the District of Columbia that claimed Facebook and Instagram were designed to hook young users at the expense of their mental health. A chunk of that money is earmarked for youth online safety and mental health initiatives and will be paid out over the next ten years, pending court approval. Meta is dangling an additional $5 billion if other major platforms match the restrictions in the settlement.

Industry observers note that meta agreed to numerous product changes, including stronger age verification, parental controls, and an end to overnight use. But few states are relying on that alone, taking matters into their own hands. California, for example, passed bipartisan legislation on September 20th, 2026, banning infinite scrolling and personalized algorithmic feeds for youth under 16.

That said, as a clinical psychologist, Yale professor, and youth mental health expert, I know the devil is in the details, not the celebratory headlines. What gets done with this money, and how quickly, is still an open question. But if states take a few real notes from the opioid settlement, they can handle this one differently.

First, we have to get real. The Meta settlement was an important exercise in accountability for technology companies, but this money will not solve the youth mental health crisis. It can't. Social media is only one thread of a much larger knot of problems affecting youth mental health. While Meta plays a role here, it is our collective responsibility to improve equity in mental health support availability, access, and quality.

In a recent development, second, one of the clearest critiques of the opioid settlements is the absence of any national requirement that states report where they spend the money. At a minimum, every state receiving Meta settlement funds should publicly share what it funds, what it's learning, and what isn't working, on a recurring timeline. Minnesota runs a public dashboard breaking down settlement spending, and North Carolina requires local governments to report spending annually through a public portal. Beyond spending transparency, with different amounts per state, implementation and outcomes transparency is also key. California, which helped lead the case, stands to receive the largest final payout, in excess of $2 billion. That puts California and other large recipient states in a position to share their implementation strategies, pilot data, and model resources that other states with smaller amounts can use.

States must also be disciplined. With healthcare budgets under pressure from federal Medicaid changes, especially for access to mental health services, the temptation to backfill budget holes is understandable. But this approach is unlikely to produce sustainable change. Even the roughly $56 billion states and localities receiving over 18 years in opioid settlements doesn't come close to covering what's been lost elsewhere, according to published analyses from the Bipartisan Policy Center’s Opioid Crisis Task Force. This money was never going to replace existing investment, only add to it. That's why at least a dozen states have written explicit restrictions into law against using opioid settlement funds to backfill existing budgets, and states handling the Meta settlement should adopt that restriction from day one.

Finally (for now), young people must be included in whatever gets built on their behalf from these dollars. Their lived experience is vital expertise, and its absence is a documented missed opportunity in the opioid settlements. According to reports, only about 7 percent of people on opioid settlement advisory committees nationally had lived experience for the crisis they were advising on. Alternatively, Washington state required at least four members with lived experience to be appointed members to the settlement committee and compensated for their work. States building out Meta settlement advisory structures should build from this model. Implementation of any solutions is certain to be more successful when young people, their communities, and priorities are centered.

Sources indicate that I don't have $12 billion settlement dollars, and neither does any single state on its own. But every state that's about to receive a piece of this Meta settlement has more control over what happens next than the opioid settlements ever gave states credit for exercising. The difference this time isn't the dollar amount. It's whether we treat the last decade of settlement spending as a cautionary tale or as a blueprint we already have in hand.

#203. Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water

📅 12 Nov 2026

Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water

Tanggal: 12 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110042549.htm

Earth may have created a substantial amount of its own water as the planet was forming, rather than relying entirely on comets, meteorites, or other objects to deliver it from space. New research published in Nature Geoscience suggests that chemical reactions between rocky pebbles and the hydrogen-rich atmosphere of the young Earth could have produced enormous quantities of water.

It has been revealed that the discovery offers a new explanation for how our planet acquired one of the most notable ingredients for life. It also raises the possibility that other rocky planets throughout the universe could generate water through similar processes, potentially making habitable worlds more common than previously thought.

Researchers at The University of Newly introduced Mexico investigated this possibility by recreating some of the extreme conditions that existed during Earth's formation. The study was led by graduate student Susmita Garai, along with Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Peter Olson. Their experiments examined what happens when rocks containing iron react with hydrogen at extremely high temperatures.

In a recent development, "Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism," explained Sharp. "In order to evaluate the possibility of 'pebble' rain' being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high-temperature experiments. Dr. Garai's efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high temperature environment of the Early Earth's atmosphere.".

A Newly introduced Explanation for the Origin of Earth's Water.

According to recent reports, for decades, scientists have debated where Earth's water originally came from. One prominent theory suggests that much of it was transported to the developing planet by icy material originating in the colder, more distant regions of the early solar system.

According to this explanation, water-rich objects, including small icy pebbles, traveled inward and eventually contributed to Earth's water supply. However, researchers have struggled to fully explain how enough of this material could have reached our planet from such great distances. There are also unresolved questions about whether this delivery process accounts for Earth's chemical composition.

It has been revealed that the fresh study investigates a different route by which water could have appeared. Instead of arriving already contained in ice or other materials, water may have been produced directly through reactions involving the rocky ingredients that built Earth and the gases surrounding it.

In a recent development, during the planet's earliest stages, countless small pieces of rock gradually came together to form a larger body. Scientists refer to this growth process as pebble accretion. As Earth gained mass, it could have accumulated a dense atmosphere containing large amounts of hydrogen, with temperatures and pressures far higher than those found on the planet today.

Under those conditions, rocky pebbles falling through the atmosphere could have triggered a remarkable chemical reaction. Hydrogen in the surrounding gas would react with iron oxide inside the silicate rocks, transforming the iron oxide into metallic iron while releasing water vapor.

Experiments Reveal Water Can Form in Minutes.

Recent findings suggest that to determine whether this process could actually occur, the researchers exposed samples of silicate rock to temperatures ranging from 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius. They conducted experiments using flowing hydrogen gas and repeated the tests with helium to provide a comparison. Each experiment ran for between 15 minutes and three hours.

The results provided strong evidence that the proposed reaction works under these extreme conditions. When the rocks were heated in hydrogen, almost 80% of their iron oxide was transformed into metallic iron, with water vapor produced during the reaction.

Industry observers note that in contrast, the researchers did not observe the same reaction when helium was used instead of hydrogen. This difference confirmed that hydrogen played a crucial role in generating the water.

The speed and scale of the reaction were especially striking. Although the scientists had expected some water to form, the results suggested that the process could have been far more productive than anticipated. When they extended their experimental findings to conditions on the early Earth, their calculations indicated that the mechanism might have generated hundreds of oceans' worth of water.

"We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans' worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 ½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have," noted Sharp.

Earth's Fiery Beginnings May Have Helped Create Its Oceans.

Recent findings suggest that these findings suggest that the conditions of Earth's formation may have actively contributed to its water supply. Rather than being entirely dependent on water delivered from elsewhere in the solar system, the growing planet may have possessed the ingredients needed to manufacture water through its own chemical reactions.

The implications extend well beyond Earth. If rocky planets around other stars develop similarly hot, hydrogen-rich atmospheres during their formation, they might also produce substantial amounts of water as rocky material accumulates.

This possibility could have important consequences for understanding how common water is across the universe. A process that naturally occurs during the formation of Earth-sized planets would mean that obtaining water might not require the right icy objects to arrive from distant regions of a planetary system.

Could Other Earth-Like Planets Make Their Own Water?

The research also adds to growing interest in pebble accretion as an explanation for how planets form. Although the concept has gained attention relatively recently, it has already helped scientists address several longstanding questions about planetary development.

It has been revealed that "The idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. It's only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation," Sharp mentioned. "And now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life.".

There are still important uncertainties to resolve. While the experiments show that rocky material can generate water when exposed to hydrogen under conditions resembling those of the early Earth, they do not establish how much of our planet's present water supply was actually produced this way. Additional research will be needed to determine the contribution of this mechanism compared with water delivered by comets, meteorites, and other sources.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important process that may have shaped Earth billions of years ago. They also suggest that the ability to produce water could be built into the formation of rocky planets themselves, opening latest possibilities for understanding where water, and perhaps life, might exist beyond our solar system.

#205. This bear’s major butt is so beautiful, it just won an award

📅 10 Nov 2026

This bear’s major butt is so beautiful, it just won an award

Tanggal: 10 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.popsci.com/environment/bear-big-butt-beautiful-award-alaska/

Published Nov 10, 2026 3:13 PM EST.

Yes, bears are substantial. Depending on the time of year and sex, the average black bear (Ursus americanus) weighs between 90 to 500 pounds. On average brown bears (Ursus arctos) can weigh between 600 to 900 pounds. However, one female black bear named Volverine is a true fat bear queen this year. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded her with the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her heft.

According to recent reports, the rangers say that this mother bear is a “true icon,” who will often pose on a rock for a long time, seemingly allowing the visitors to Anan Wildlife Observatory to take photos. She is regarded as one of the most beautiful bears at Anan, with a chest patch shaped like the letter V. Volverine is also on the bigger end of the black bear spectrum, with a potato-shaped body, and an especially round butt. Her fishing skills made her one of the largest bears of the 2026 season—and a dominant matriarch.

“Our rangers love to see a fat female bear because that could mean cubs next year!” the rangers write. “Bears have what’s called delayed implantation, meaning they mate in the spring, and IF they get fat enough, the embryos implant in the fall.”.

Wishing Volverine and all of the bears the best this winter season.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are presently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. The run is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

Sources indicate that according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks. Volverine would fit right in with Katmai’s chunky brown bears, despite the fact that black bears tend to be a bit smaller.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of what they are up to 24/7.

#206. Driven: Porsche 911 Challenge Is a More Accessible Race Car

📅 12 Nov 2026

Driven: Porsche 911 Challenge Is a More Accessible Race Car

Tanggal: 12 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.roadandtrack.com/reviews/a74270482/driven-porsche-911-challenge/

It has been revealed that many track cars are intimidating, to say the least. Not Porsche’s latest.

Sources indicate that next year will mark the 40th running of the Porsche Mobil 1 Supercup, the one-make race series so ubiquitous you hardly need either Porsche or 911 qualifiers for somebody to know what you mean by “Cup car.” Like other sports cars with long histories, the further you go back in time, the more similar the racing 911 is to the roadgoing version. Likewise, the further forward you move, the more they diverge.

Early 964 Cup cars are, like Ferrari’s 355 Challenge, road legal with normal VIN codes. They were stripped, caged versions of standard Carreras. I’m leaving out a lot of hardworking engineers’ tweaks here, but the point is that there was a time that driving a Cup car felt mostly like a normal car with more noise, fewer comforts, and better safety equipment. The 1999 996-generation Cup still used a coded key and had a normal clutch and an H-pattern 6-speed—it was just a very sticky GT3. But the 997 generation of 2005 was the fork in the road, introducing a sequential gearbox. The 2013 991-gen brought in a motorsport engine-management system and electronics. And the 992 generation that races today nominally resembles a 911 but operates nothing like one and requires a team to run it.

It has been revealed that I tried the 992 Cup Car. It is incredibly intimidating. I do not have what it takes to be successful in a car like that, and I would not want to have to round up a posse to go for a drive, even if the performance is staggering. Instead what I really want, as do many other amateur and wannabe racers, is a race car that closely resembles their road car. Hence the popularity of the GT3 RS. If the car never leaves the track property, why get a GT3 RS when you could get an Oreca LMP for $100k less? Because it’s not really about being street legal; it’s about being approachable and turnkey.

The car for regular weekend warriors used to be the GT4/RS Clubsport, but sadly, the 718-generation Cayman is now dead and buried. Earlier this year, rumors swirled that Porsche was prepping a 911 GT4 to take the Cayman’s place, and the story ran alongside photos of a racy-looking camouflaged 992 GT3. It turns out that Porsche is going GT4 racing with the 911, but that will be a modified Cup car, not the one from those pictures. Instead, the images were of the car you see here, the new 911 Challenge. Essentially, it’s the old GT3 Cup car concept for today’s country-club weekend warriors: an upfitted, stripped, and caged GT3 road car.

Recent findings suggest that A roll cage can only make a car so approachable, but once I’d stopped and crawled into the comfy seat, things got familiar rapidly, as I was looking at the complete 992-generation dashboard, gauge cluster, and center console. The steering wheel is straight out of the GT3 RS (though without an airbag installed). After strapping in with the multipoint harnesses,I pressed the original start button on the left, and the 4.0-liter flat-six fired just like a standard GT3. The Challenge retains the factory heating and ventilation; the road car’s touchscreen display is gone, replaced by a blank panel with emergency cutoff and fire switches.

According to recent reports, mechanically, it’s barely changed from the GT3. The engine makes six more horsepower, now 508 hp total, thanks to a race-specific exhaust setup. But it still uses the standard, seven-speed PDK dual-clutch transmission, so you can just put it in drive if you prefer, or shift using the paddles.

My drive in the Challenge was brief. Just four laps around the 2.5-mile Circuit Ricardo Tormo, following on from my four-car Manthey test. For context, with factory race driver Timo Bernhard driving this circuit, the Challenge almost perfectly splits the range: 4.6 seconds per lap slower than a Cup, and 5.2 seconds quicker than a GT3 Weissach. Notably, it’s also 1.6 seconds quicker per lap than the GT3 RS Manthey. Where it gets interesting is in the details.

According to recent reports, A GT3 RS Manthey is on road-legal tires but with enormous downforce. The Challenge is on slicks but with the same aero package as a standard GT3.

So if you’re willing to throw away street legality, for $275,000 (less than the cost of many standard GT3s) you can go far quicker on a track than you could with the fastest road-legal 911 you can buy, the Manthey GT3 RS, which would knock on the door of half a million dollars.

It has been revealed that everything about the Challenge is easy. As long as you’re reasonably comfortable on a slick tire, the rest of the car comes directly to you. The Challenge is far more reliant on mechanical grip than downforce, so you can start learning the car by going much quicker through hairpins than you ever have before, rather than having to learn it by going full send over a blind crest in sixth gear, with potentially scary consequences.

In a recent development, likewise, because there isn’t 2200 pounds of downforce, the Challenge isn’t sprung too stiffly, so you don’t take abuse on bumpy curbing. The knobs for traction control and PTV work essentially the same as the GT3 RS, just with latest programming specific to the Challenge.

I’m not going to pretend, in five laps, to have a thorough understanding of the dynamics of the 911 Challenge, or to say that I took it to its limit. I had just enough time to get comfortable, which is more than I can say about other race cars.

What I did have was an incredible time on the track. The Challenge is the kind of car that inspired me to want to push it harder, but the “race car” bits of it disappeared into the background, so I could focus on things happening outside rather than things inside. It was instantly comfortable and familiar, and a place I could spend all day. Three-hour double stint in an enduro? That would be no problem. Also, possible thanks to the 29-gallon fuel cell.

There will be a one-make series for the 911 Challenge, and initially Porsche wants to sell them to folks who intend to enter, but that’s not really the point—this is the 911 race car that most 911 owners actually want. It is a fun, flexible, approachable, and fizzy experience that elevates what they already love about the 911 and can race if they want to, but that won’t require a whole team if they just want to rip off a few laps after work. And for less money than the road car, not more.

It’s the race car for people who want their race car to feel like a 911, not like a corporation.

#208. NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

📅 11 Nov 2026

NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

Tanggal: 11 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110042546.htm

Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, reaching one of its largest sizes on record. Despite the striking increase, scientists from NASA and NOAA say Earth's protective ozone layer is continuing its gradual recovery and remains on track to heal later this century.

It has been revealed that the 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a large circulation of winds that influences atmospheric conditions over Antarctica. They also emphasized that international efforts to reduce harmful chemicals have prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

Recent findings suggest that between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was at its seasonal peak, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone in the stratosphere because it serves as Earth's natural "sunscreen," protecting living organisms from dangerous solar radiation. Unlike this beneficial layer high in the atmosphere, ozone near Earth's surface is a pollutant frequently associated with human activities.

Antarctica's Ozone Hole Reaches Its Largest Size in a Decade.

The ozone hole reached its maximum extent on September 18, spreading across 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). This was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

Industry observers note that "The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing," stated Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA's ozone research team at the agency's Goddard Space Flight Center. "But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven't seen in a decade.".

Sources indicate that although the hole expanded to an extraordinary size, the results also demonstrate the benefits of decades of international environmental protections. Without reductions in chemicals known to destroy ozone, the affected area could have been substantially greater.

"The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak," Newman noted.

How a Powerful Polar Vortex Accelerates Ozone Loss.

Ozone depletion begins with chemicals released through human activities, particularly compounds containing chlorine and bromine. Atmospheric circulation transports these substances into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet radiation breaks them apart. The released chlorine and bromine atoms then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in Antarctic stratospheric clouds, leading to the destruction of ozone.

In a recent development, A major factor in this process is the stratospheric polar vortex, a seasonal band of strong winds that circles Antarctica. This circulation traps extremely cold air over the region, allowing the formation of the special clouds that help trigger ozone destruction. When the vortex becomes unusually strong or expansive, conditions favorable for ozone loss can persist across a larger area.

Industry observers note that in 2026, atmospheric disturbances that would normally weaken the vortex were unusually subdued. This allowed the circulation to remain powerful and helped create a broader region where ozone could be destroyed.

Industry observers note that "The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September," noted Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. "That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.".

NASA and NOAA Measure the 2026 Ozone Hole.

Despite its exceptional geographic size, the 2026 ozone hole did not experience the same extreme levels of ozone loss observed during record-breaking events 10 or 20 years earlier.

To measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers debuted instruments attached to weather balloons from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected readings using the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical device designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations showed that ozone levels directly above the South Pole fell to their lowest reading of 2026 on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

Industry observers note that the Dobson unit is the standard measurement used to describe the total amount of ozone above a particular location. To illustrate the scale, 100 Dobson units would produce a layer of ozone just 1 millimeter thick, approximately the thickness of a dime, if all the ozone in the atmospheric column were compressed to standard temperature and pressure at sea level. The lowest ozone concentration ever measured over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.

Satellites provide another essential source of information. Since 1979, spaceborne instruments have helped scientists observe changes in the ozone layer and track its condition over time. The 2026 measurements included data from NASA's Aura satellite, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, a joint NASA and NOAA mission.

Why Earth's Ozone Layer Is Still Recovering.

In a recent development, scientists say the latest observations reinforce evidence that international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals are working. Much of that progress can be traced to the Montreal Protocol, a global agreement adopted in 1987 to phase out substances responsible for damaging the ozone layer.

In a recent development, under the agreement, countries committed to replacing harmful compounds such as chlorofluorocarbons with alternatives that pose less danger to atmospheric ozone. According to Stephen Montzka, a senior scientist at NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory, chlorine concentrations in the Antarctic stratosphere associated with ozone-depleting chemicals have declined by approximately one-third compared with their peak levels in the 1980s.

Recent findings suggest that these reductions are significant because chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once common in refrigerators, air conditioning systems, building insulation, and other everyday products. Although many of these substances have been phased out, they can remain in the atmosphere for decades. Additional emissions can also occur when older equipment, materials, and landfill waste release chemicals that were manufactured years ago.

Sources indicate that because these compounds break down so slowly, repairing the ozone layer takes many decades. Nevertheless, continued monitoring by NASA and NOAA indicates that the long-term recovery is progressing. Even with unusually large seasonal ozone holes such as the one observed in 2026, scientists expect the Antarctic ozone hole to recover by the 2070s.

The latest findings illustrate how exceptional atmospheric conditions can temporarily produce severe ozone depletion without reversing decades of environmental progress. They also highlight the lasting impact of international cooperation in protecting Earth's atmosphere.

#209. Breaking: How Gossip Is Good for Us

📅 13 Nov 2026

Breaking: How Gossip Is Good for Us

Tanggal: 13 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-stories-of-our-lives/202611/how-gossip-is-good-for-us

In a recent development, after years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Recent findings suggest that self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

As the saying goes, “If you don’t have anything good to say, don’t say anything.” But in the words of Alice Roosevelt Longworth, perhaps more of us prefer: “If you can’t say something good about someone, sit right here by me.” After all, deep down, we all love some good gossip, don’t we?

Sources indicate that in fact, by some estimates of everyday conversations, upwards of 65 percent of what we talk about involves people and social interactions, both self-disclosures and information about others’ escapades. And “gossip,” defined as the telling of stories about the everyday adventures of the people in our lives that we tell to, with, and about others, began deep in our evolutionary history. As soon as we began to use language, we started to gossip!

In a recent development, as we gather around the holiday table this year with friends and family we may not have seen in a while, we will share stories of our lives, stories of their lives, and stories of our friends and family not able to be present at the table. The good news is that this is actually good for us. Whereas gossip has a bad reputation, in fact, it serves a critical function in weaving our lives together and keeping our social groups connected.

In a recent development, dunbar, an evolutionary anthropologist, argues that gossip began very early in our ancestral history. Living in larger social groups benefited our survival, and gossip is a necessary part of keeping larger social groups cohesive. Through sharing stories about how Uncle Joe and Aunt Louise are settling into their upcoming living arrangements in Timbuktu, we maintain a sense of belonging to the group, and this sense of belonging adds to our own sense of meaning and purpose in life. When we feel socially isolated, we actually experience physical pain; Williams and Nida show experimentally that social exclusion for as little as two minutes leads to physiological pain responses and emotional distress, and longer periods of social isolation can result in depression, helplessness, and alienation. Maintaining social connections by integrating our lives with others through stories and gossip brings us together and creates a sense of well-being.

Gossip also serves to help us with advice and discussion of possible problems—if you are thinking about changing jobs, a story about cousin Bill who just did that could provide invaluable information as you consider your options. With my colleagues David Pillemer and Dorthe Thomsen, we showed how these kinds of vicarious stories, stories about other people that resonate with who we are, can promote successful adaptation, help us make good decisions, and teach us morals and values for how to live a good life. We don’t have to experience things directly to learn from them. We can learn from the experiences of others through gossip.

Vicarious stories are particularly prominent in family storytelling. Alongside stories of shared family experiences, such as the Thanksgiving when Dad dropped the turkey on the kitchen floor, and we all had to eat hot dogs, are stories of the family past: stories about parents growing up or grandparents, aunts, and uncles. When the younger generation hears these stories, whether from the person who experienced them (“When I was your age….”) or third-hand as gossip (“Your grandfather loved Thanksgiving, and every year, he would invite friends from work who had nowhere else to go”), these stories become frameworks for how to live a life. Gossip provides us with maps for how the world works.

According to recent reports, of course, there is a dark side to gossip. As Dores-Cruz and colleagues point out, gossip can be used to purposely damage someone else’s reputation, perhaps in the service of self-aggrandizement, and thus can lead to mistrust within the group. They conducted a series of studies to assess people’s motivations and tendency to gossip, especially when the person being gossiped about was experimentally manipulated to be a victim of malicious rumors. They found that group members were more likely to gossip when a group member was being maliciously maligned in order to protect the victim’s reputation. At the same time, people are motivated to spread the word about members of the group who violate norms, suggesting that gossip serves to keep everyone in line. Gossip is a little bit like herding sheep, making sure the group maintains positive bonds and bringing those who deviate from this back into the fold.

This holiday season, there will be gossip! I will spend Thanksgiving with my “framily” (friends and family), and there will be some dear framily we will miss who are not able to be there. But we will gossip! “Did you hear about so-and-so?” and “Let me tell you what happened…” We will laugh, and we will shed tears. And we will cement our bonds. So, this Thanksgiving, if you have something juicy to tell, come sit by me!

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

Recent findings suggest that by 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:.

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

In a recent development, coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:.

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

Sources indicate that however, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:.

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she stated.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

Sources indicate that “Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:.

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

Recent findings suggest that she also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an crucial factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#212. Latest Update: What the Recent Tech Outage Can Teach Us About Balance

Latest Update: What the Recent Tech Outage Can Teach Us About Balance

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

It has been revealed that self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

As I write this, parts of North America and Europe are experiencing a Microsoft outage that is affecting certain parts of the cloud infrastructure, particularly office communication services such as Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 360. While this is certainly causing disruption and inconvenience in many corporate and business settings, it may also be reminding us of an important reality that we often talk about but rarely implement: work-life balance.

Industry observers note that in the United States, it has long been reported that workers struggle with creating healthy boundaries between their lives and their jobs, and a 2025 study found that a staggering 66 percent of American workers reported having experienced “some degree of burnout” in the past year (Robinson, 2025). Additionally, 2024 research indicated that 44 percent of employees and 53 percent of supervisors experienced burnout at their jobs (Malinsky, 2022). It is no secret that many of us struggle to find the “sweet spot” between work and the rest of our lives. Increasingly, this disparity between work and life is being seen as a larger problem that, according to a 2021 study, is more than “an individual-level phenomenon,” and is “a societal concern that necessitates systematic support from a wider range of stakeholders” (Fan, Yuyang, et al., 2021).

Along with the statistical evidence, we can find plenty of anecdotal proof that this is a widespread problem: you would be hard-pressed to find a person who does not report some level of exhaustion or burnout related to their career, myself and those I know being no exception. But if it is such an concern, why are we unable to see something like this Microsoft outage as a gift rather than an inconvenience? I would argue that it has to do with our longstanding relationship with work and our misprioritization of its importance. American attitudes about work have long been centered around productivity, busyness, results, and multitasking. Words like “balance” are simply not part of our career-related vernacular.

When something like a technology outage forces us to let go of our usual outcome-orientation towards our jobs, it can feel odd and somehow “wrong.” Looking at social media comments today, I am seeing more that speak to how annoying and inconvenient this outage is and less that speak to it allowing for a slower workday or an (albeit forced) opportunity to not work as hard. But perhaps we can learn from today’s widespread inconvenience. In some workplaces, you are unable to send or answer emails, communicate as usual, or access cloud-related platforms. In one sense, this is frustrating. In another, it is permission not to do these things that, let’s be honest, are often done from home, from the dinner table, at unhealthy hours, in the midst of other life activities, and at the cost of mindfulness and presence in our lives. I am not suggesting that tech outages are good for business, but rather that they can remind us that creating space between work and life is necessary for our overall well-being.

Sometimes inconveniences can be opportunities. In Buddhist philosophy, the concept that the “obstacle is the path” is applicable to today’s inconvenience. The obstacle (not being able to access the usual work platforms) is the path to allowing ourselves to slow down and create some space between work and life—at least for a day or two.
